The apps include AI scenes such as “bedroom rape” and “threatening knife,” where a man holds a knife to a woman’s neck.

I feel like this going to be a never ending cat and mouse game. Much like Apple has always had with jailbreaks.

Wired says that the network is “hiding in plain sight,” thanks to thousands of video ads for them published on Facebook and Instagram. Some of the apps have been around for a year and have passed review by Apple, Google, and Meta despite each having clear policies prohibiting harmful deepfake content.

Bait-and-switch tactics were used to pass app review. The apps normally show benign content, but a server check can activate the hidden features. Downloading the app after tapping an ad for the deepfake functionality on Meta platforms appears to be one of the triggers. Dozens of pornography photo and video templates can then be downloaded, with credits purchased to generate deepfakes from user-uploaded photos.

Apple removed 19 apps after Wired shared details.

We review every app before it’s published, and these apps complied with our rules when we reviewed them. #3383. How to Try 'Audio Intelligence' on Your Apple Watch Early

It has been a big year for Apple. There's a new CEO, prices have increased across the board, and there's been a seemingly endless rollout of new devices, including two new Apple Watches: the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. All things considered, these watches offer only minor upgrades over the previous models, shipping with new heart rate monitors and the latest S11 processor. But one of the biggest new watch features, "Audio Intelligence," is also the most controversial—and it's rolling out in beta today.

Audio Intelligence is Apple's branding for a new set of features exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4. These features use the new Apple Watches' hardware, along with on-device and cloud-based AI, for tasks like sound and music identification as well as dictation. "Sound Recognition" can alert you to important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, while "Music Recognition" can automatically display songs playing around you—but these aren't the features you'll hear talked about in discussions of Audio Intelligence.

Rather, everyone is up in arms about "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap." These Audio Intelligence features passively "listen" to your conversations throughout the day, and, using AI, deliver summaries of what was said. When you double-click your Apple Watch's crown to use Live Rewind, you'll get a loose transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation it overheard, while Siri Recap can show summaries of all your in-person chats throughout the day. You can even configure a schedule for when your watch is "listening" for recaps—e.g., only run during work hours. Apple suggests each is intended to help jog your memory; maybe you use Siri Recap to remember important discussions you had that morning, while Live Rewind is meant for moments where you forget what someone just said. (As opposed to asking them to repeat themselves, I suppose.)

Apple's claims may or may not assuage your fears, but it seems the company is pushing on ahead regardless. Apple is releasing Audio Intelligence as part of iOS 27.3, which launches in beta on Tuesday. If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you can try it out today, assuming you enroll in Apple's latest beta version.

To do so, you'll need to sign up for the Apple Developer program, since iOS 27.3 is rolling out first for devs. This program used to require a $99 fee, but you can skip it now if you opt for the free account. Once you enroll your Apple Account in this program, you can open your iPhone, head to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, and choose "iOS 27 Developer Beta." Go back one page, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install iOS 27.3 when it's available.

Don't assume AI will be unbiased when it comes to data centers

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Ask ChatGPT about a major AI data center project, and you might get a fairly straightforward description of what it is, where it's being built and how much companies plan to invest. Ask Google AI about the same project's challenges, and you could walk away with a much more negative impression.

That's one of the findings from new research published by Five Blocks, a digital reputation management company that examined how eight AI engines describe 25 of America's largest AI data center projects.

The researchers found that none of the 1,200 general project descriptions they rated were negative. But when the question changed to what challenges each project faced, 55% of answers were classified as negative.

The differences between AI platforms were even more surprising. Google AI Mode produced negative answers to the challenges question 88% of the time, compared with just 6% for ChatGPT.

As AI data centers expand across the country, and Americans question what these projects could mean for their electricity bills, water supplies and neighborhoods, the research raises an important issue. The AI tool someone chooses, along with the words they type, can dramatically change the information they receive.

For the first study, published Tuesday, Five Blocks asked eight AI engines two questions about 25 major U.S. data center projects every day throughout September 2026.

The prompts were deliberately simple: "Tell me about [project]" and "What challenges does [project] face?"

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

That small change produced dramatically different results. General descriptions tended to emphasize a project's size, investment and technological ambitions. When asked about challenges, however, AI engines were much more likely to focus on problems or opposition surrounding the developments.

Some projects attracted considerably more negative responses than others.

More than 80% of challenge-related answers about Fermi America's Project Matador, Meta's Hyperion, Stargate and Vantage's Lighthouse were rated negative.

By comparison, Amazon's Project Rainier and Microsoft's Fairwater project in Atlanta received negative responses roughly 20% of the time or less.

Even projects belonging to the same company received different treatment. Microsoft's Atlanta development had a negative-response rate of about one in five, while its Wisconsin project approached seven in ten.

One particularly striking finding involved Microsoft's own AI assistant. According to the study, Copilot's general description of the Fairwater Wisconsin project incorrectly claimed the project didn't exist until September 24.

The results suggest that AI-generated descriptions aren't necessarily reliable snapshots of a project's current status, and different platforms may emphasize completely different aspects of the same development.

1. The neutral question: Tell me about Microsoft's Fairwater AI data center project in Wisconsin.Both agents immediately described the benefits of the AI data centers. Gemini called it a "purpose-built" campus while ChatGPT highlighted the amount of jobs the center would bring to the community. 2. The challenges question: What challenges does Microsoft's Fairwater AI data center project in Wisconsin face?While both agents shared the negative impact of data centers, both highlighted the "ambitions" of Microsoft. 3. The homeowner question: I live near Microsoft's Fairwater data center project in Wisconsin. Should I be worried about my electricity bills, water supply or property value? I found it annoying that ChatGPT created an image of the data center each time. It sort of glossed over any concerns and then created a survey about how close to the data center I live. Gemini told me that many fears were "over stated."

A second Five Blocks study, published November 2, examined how AI engines discuss data centers more broadly.

Researchers asked eight AI engines six questions about data centers every day throughout September, then compared their answers with responses about other energy and infrastructure developments, including pipelines, fracking sites, nuclear power plants, wind farms and solar farms.

They found that 83% of answers discussing data centers and their neighbors offered what the researchers classified as one-sided criticism. That was the same percentage recorded for oil and gas pipelines, but considerably higher than the 35% reported for solar farms.

Even questions specifically about economic benefits frequently produced qualified responses. Seven in ten answers about data center economic benefits included a counterpoint, compared with fewer than two in ten for solar farms.

Tax incentives were another recurring theme. Approximately two-thirds of answers concerning data centers and neighboring communities mentioned tax breaks, while nearly one-quarter brought up nondisclosure agreements.

ChatGPT was also an outlier in this study. According to Five Blocks, it was the only AI engine that consistently provided balanced responses about community concerns, while the other seven were rated as one-sided in nearly every evaluated answer.

There's an important difference between an AI chatbot giving a negative answer and giving an inaccurate one.

If someone asks about the challenges facing a proposed data center, it's reasonable for an AI assistant to discuss potential electricity demand, water consumption, local opposition and infrastructure costs.

Those are legitimate issues that communities and policymakers are already debating. And that's why the research illustrates a problem for anyone using AI to understand a complicated issue. Two systems can provide very different impressions without necessarily inventing any facts.

If you're researching a data center proposed near your home, relying on one AI-generated summary probably isn't enough.

A more useful approach is to ask questions that encourage the chatbot to consider different sides of the issue. For example, rather than simply asking what a data center project is, try this prompt:

Explain the potential benefits and drawbacks of the proposed data center in my community. Include its possible effects on electricity rates, water use, jobs, tax revenue and nearby residents. Separate confirmed facts from estimates and provide links to original sources.

You can also ask the chatbot to identify information it couldn't verify, explain which claims come from the developer and which come from independent sources, and distinguish between proposed plans and approved construction.

For a second opinion, run the same prompt through another AI platform. If ChatGPT and Google AI produce noticeably different answers, that's a reason to investigate the underlying sources rather than assume one chatbot must be correct.

The Five Blocks research shows why turning to AI for answers is an approach deserves caution, particularly on the topic of data centers. As more data centers are proposed around the world and in our own neighborhoods, it's best to get information from your town's own local planning board documents, utility filings and public hearing records. AI can help you do this research, but be sure to fact-check it on your own rather than relying on AI summaries.

Nobody wants their smart home turning stupid overnight. Here's how to future-proof yours

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, smart homes are hot right now – apps and AI are weaving their way into every facet of home life, from turning on the lights and checking security footage to adjusting the thermostat and managing your family's hectic schedule.

"Smart" doesn't always mean... smart, though, and embedding technology into everyday household appliances can sometimes backfire.

Take Neato Robotics' robot vacuum, for example, which ceased operating in May 2023 before its parent company, Vorwerk, phased out cloud services from October 2025 – leaving owners without app controls.

Some might laugh and point to perfectly functional "dumb" vacuums, but Neato is hardly alone in this brave new world: smart lights, cameras, thermostats, and myriad other gadgets can depend on services that might vanish overnight.

In 2026, when almost everything comes with an app or cloud features, buying smart is becoming increasingly important – especially if you want to avoid gadgets with a hidden expiration date.

While 'the cloud' might be nice branding, the reality is that many smart gadgets rely on physical infrastructure operated by manufacturers or third-party providers to process commands, manage features, and so on.

For cloud-dependent gadgets, then, the hardware isn't always quite as independent as it might seem.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The situation is exemplified by Belkin, one of the top smart home accessory makers. Back in January, Belkin discontinued cloud services for numerous WeMo products, affecting smart plugs and other household gadgets.

As a result, the WeMo app stopped working, alongside cloud-dependent features like Google Assistant integration. For anyone who'd paid good money for these gadgets, it was subpar, to say the least.

Some devices, however, got a reprieve of sorts: those already configured with Apple's HomeKit before the shutdown could continue working locally.

Even some really popular devices from large companies haven't escaped this. As Google migrated Nest devices to its platform, it discontinued support for some of the original Nest Learning Thermostats.

Not every gadget is like this, though. Some can communicate directly over your home network, keeping smart lights and plugs responding to commands without an internet connection or their manufacturer's servers – provided the local controller and network still work.

Enter Matter, a smart home standard backed by tech giants like Apple, Google, and Amazon that allows compatible gadgets to communicate locally with a controller, without relying on proprietary cloud services for basic functions.

Sadly, Matter is not a panacea. Some manufacturer-specific features, firmware updates, and remote access may still require internet connectivity, and certain products need an app or account for their initial setup.

Local control can offer a good amount of protection from a capricious company that cuts off your gadgets, but choosing the right devices in the first place is still key.

If you're buying new smart home gadgets, there are four things worth checking before handing over your money. We'll explore each of them in turn.

Devices that offer local control and Matter compatibility are a great place to start, as they're less vulnerable to manufacturers switching off cloud services. In our guide to the best smart plugs, options like the TP-Link Tapo Smart Plug Mini support Matter out of the box.

When the internet goes down, what happens? Can you still turn on the lights or adjust your heating? These are some of the key questions that will help when things go awry. Prioritize essential functions that can work independently, especially when it comes to expensive appliances or security equipment.

Choosing a subscription-free camera with local recording, for example, could save you a lot of headaches – although it's worth checking whether you can still access your footage without the manufacturer's app.

Research a manufacturer's support policies and commitments before buying, so you won't be caught out. A heavily discounted gadget might seem like an attractive option – only for you to discover it's already several years into its support period.

It's also worth checking the company's track record of withdrawing support or shutting down services; a promise of security updates isn't necessarily a guarantee that cloud features will survive.

Check whether your device can work with another ecosystem or controller – a compatible smart home hub could be useful here. As we saw with Belkin, existing HomeKit setups survived the shutdown, but owners couldn't configure their devices again afterwards.

Being able to reset and reconnect your gadgets without the manufacturer's servers could save you a lot of stress down the line

This smart plug from TP-Link is one of the best smart plugs for its small size and affordable price. It supports Matter, so it works across all major smart home ecosystems. Plus, its feature-packed app monitors energy usage and lets you schedule when the connected devices turn on and off. A great way to make any appliance "smart."

Smart home gadgets can make everyday life a lot more convenient, offering quick ways to control all manner of household devices, and there's no reason to be put off by the occasional corporate shutdown.

No connected gadget is entirely future-proof, and even the biggest tech companies can discontinue services – especially for older products with relatively few users.

A sensible approach, then, is to pick gadgets that can retain their essential functions even if the manufacturer's cloud services disappear.

A truly smart home is one that can still switch off the lights even when someone switches off the server.

#3372. ‘Don’t Get Rid of MAGA!’: Some Young Republicans Are Sticking by Trump After Blowout Loss

To his credit, the New York Young Republican Club’s designated elections guy started strong.

“Your Republican leaders have failed you!” Mario Nicoletto, 25, the campaign committee chairman for the tri-state area’s biggest and loudest conservative youth group, thundered from a lectern dragged out into the middle of the club’s living room — a cozy space stuffed with leather couches and framed photos of the slain activist Charlie Kirk. “The boomers, the millennials, the Gen X, the folks in D.C. who do not care about us — they have failed us!”

To Nicoletto’s right, TVs set to Fox News flashed undeniably dismal numbers: Republicans down in Ohio, in Michigan, god — even in Texas. Nicoletto went on, telling the few dozen club regulars in attendance that he would “spend every waking moment” in the coming years signing up new Republican voters. “We are going to take the city back in 2028!”

There was a smattering of applause, a few hoots. The TVs were all on mute, and silence crept into the room. “Let’s get some music on!” Nicoletto said, relinquishing the mic.

At 25 years old, Tuesday night was Nicoletto’s first real taste of defeat. In one of the most disastrous midterm elections in history, Donald Trump’s Republican Party was wiped almost entirely off the map in several states. As of Wednesday morning, Senate seats in Maine, Iowa, Ohio, Texas, South Carolina, and North Carolina have flipped blue, and the president has been stripped of his majority in both chambers of Congress. Almost immediately, Trump lashed out, placing the blame for the catastrophe anywhere but on himself — despite the war in Iran, brutal tariffs, a stagnant economy, and skyrocketing gas prices. Young people everywhere, including several I spoke to on election night, call this multi-faceted clusterfuck “the affordability issue.”

As results started to come in, I chatted with Alexis, a young woman who had joined the club a few years ago.   Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

“I’m 26. I wanna buy a house, I want to have a family — I can’t do those things,” she said. “I’d like to see the party just talk about that more — and more than just talk about it, figure out a way to help us!”

Alexis thought that Donald Trump had done a great job of this in the 2024 election. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, she said, a Democratic Socialist, had also focused on affordability and won big from the other side. But in 2026, she says, Republicans were at a loss for any kind of coherent message.

“The immigration thing, it indirectly helps,” Alexis said, referring to Trump’s deportation agenda. “That’s great, that’s cool… but then we’re going to war with Iran! I wish I could be in the room when they made that call to do that. It’s just like, ‘What the hell were you thinking?’”

I couldn’t blame Alexis for her exasperation. She’d spent most of the night thus far running a gauntlet of press — at least three different Scandinavian writers and a Japanese TV crew — all of whom wanted to know “how she was feeling.” I didn’t bother to ask that question, as the vibes in the room basically spoke for themselves. The people who were watching the TVs looked glum. Everyone else was mostly focused on drinking, and looked to be having a fine time.

The question I was asking was what comes next. Trump has two more years in the White House, and then the GOP has to make a choice. Republican strategists I’d talked to last month — the older, sober, grizzled types, at least — had predicted this kind of blowout loss and warned that the party was headed for a “reckoning.” Some seemed gleeful that the Trump era was ending, the siren song of neo-conservatism once again sounding faintly on the wind. But the young people in the Manhattan clubhouse were part of a different movement — MAGA — and no matter how bad their losses got, they weren’t ready to let it, or its leader, take the blame. Related Content Is Mississippi Really About to Elect a Democratic Senator? How Abdul El-Sayed Overcame the Hate and Won Big in Michigan Of Course 'Choosin' Texas' Is the Soundtrack to Texas' Political Revolution The Midterms' Biggest Loser Is Elon Musk

“Life takes all of us at a certain point,” says Becky Oliveira, 25, the club’s design chairwoman and “first lady” who is engaged to club president Stefano Forte. “I see no reason to push him out the door when there’s still work to do. This donor class, these old-guard advisers, this old-guard ecosystem that exists around him, is what needs to be taken out.”

Like many of her peers, Oliveira is protective of Trump — after all, he has been the singular figure of conservative politics for her entire adult life. The dismay in the room, then, stemmed less from the electoral losses than the existential fear that their wing of the party — the brash, radical, Trump-loving new right — would find itself cast back into the wilds, alone and adrift as their political party was reclaimed by the kind of neo-con wonks who dominated the Republican side of the swamp until 2016.

This is the secret of the young Republican movement. For every die-hard ideologue, there are more than a handful of people who really just want to be able to hang out with likeminded friends: people who like the same memes and laugh at the same jokes that might rub people in New York’s overwhelmingly liberal young adult monoculture the wrong way. Sure, some of them are deeply devoted to a specific (and sometimes dark) vision of right-wing governance, but a lot more just want to be able to talk shit about their annoying coworkers and mainstream Democrats in a city famous for libbing out.

“I don’t know how many people I’ve met [through the club] that are like, ‘Oh my gosh, I can’t believe I can have normal conversations,’” Oliveira said. “That doesn’t change regardless of who wins nationally. When they come here they find kinship and solace.”

In two presidential elections, at least, Trump turned that sense of belonging into massive electoral success — a sense of purpose, and power, and movement that many young Republicans will do anything to preserve. If the RINOs and fuddy-duddy neo-cons take back the party, the young Republicans will feel cut off from the free-wheeling culture of based memes and swamp-draining that helped them feel, for the first time in most of their lives, as if they had political power and agency.

“I don’t want to get rid of MAGA! If they scapegoat the only thing that’s been getting them votes the past decade, then the party’s going to become irrelevant,” Nicoletto said. “We need to stand with Trump — no matter how bad things get.” Trending Stories Trump's Bizarre Journey Through the Stages of Grief as Democrats Dominated the Midterms Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner Did an AMA About That Shower Scene, His Sniffing, and ‘You Can See Everything’ Dane Cook’s Brother Robbed Him Blind. Now He’s Rebuilding His Life — And Gunning for a Comeback Trump Is Already Crying That He’s Not to Blame for Republican Wipeout

Still, as the results came in, Nicoletto wasn’t entirely sure “how bad things get” could be.

“I have never seen an election of this scope, and this scale,” he said. “What comes next is a mystery to me.”

#3371. Why I'd Choose the Oura Ring 5 Over the Cheaper Ultrahuman Pro

Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro is now officially on sale in the U.S., which makes this the perfect time to consider how this new device compares to the reigning champ in the smart ring market, the Oura Ring 5. Here's the short answer: While there’s a lot to like in the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, ultimately I think the Oura Ring 5 is just better at doing its job.

I’ve spent plenty of time with both rings, and admittedly, many of the differences between the two will come down to personal preference—for example, do you like the biohacking concept and the “next best actions” suggestions in the Ultrahuman app, or do you favor the soothing vibes of the Oura app? But when it comes to the devices themselves, there are big differences between them in terms of size, cost, and overall ease of use. Here’s my take on each, and why Oura is still my top choice.

The Oura Ring 5 is impressively small, and when you have to wear something on your finger, size matters a lot—and generally, smaller is better. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I’ve ever worn. I have a ton of photos here comparing it in size to other smart rings (including RingConn, older Oura rings, and an older Ultrahuman); suffice it to say, the Oura Ring 5 wins this category easily.

When it comes to the interior fit, both rings are similar: mostly smooth on the inside, without any intrusive bumps. But considering the overall shape and feel, the Oura Ring 5 is just more comfortable to wear throughout an entire day.

The Oura Ring 5 comes with a plug-in charger, which isn’t very convenient, but will get the job done. You can buy a slim, rounded charging case that easily fits in your pocket for $99. You need to match the size of the case to the size of your ring, and the charging case is not compatible with earlier versions of the device. It’s good for 30 days of charge, according to Oura.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro comes with a charging case that is heavy and bulky with prominent corners, but good for an extra 45 days of battery life. The case fits any size of Ultrahuman Ring Pro, but is not compatible with previous versions. You can have the case play sounds if you’ve misplaced it.

The Ultrahuman ring lasts slightly longer on a charge: eight to 10 days, according to the company, versus six to nine for the Oura Ring 5. The Ultrahuman ring also has several different battery modes, with “chill mode” lasting me about two weeks.

To sum up: the Ultrahuman ring lasts longer on a charge and has more capacity in its charging case. You also get the charging case for free. But the Oura Ring 5’s charging case is smaller and much easier to carry around. Once again, we’re looking at two decent options: The Oura case is more expensive for what you get, but it’s also nicer to use.

Oura is the most expensive smart ring out there, and it requires a subscription. That makes it the priciest option, giving Ultrahuman an opening to beat it simply by virtue of being cheaper. But this one is closer to a wash, depending on the choices you make. If you’re looking for the cheapest possible smart ring, well, you’d probably end up with something else entirely, like a RingConn Air. But between the Oura Ring 5 and the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, the latter is cheaper than the Oura Ring 5...but only if you’re saying no to all the extras. Let me break it down.

The Oura Ring 5 costs $399 for the shiny black and silver models, and $499 for gold, rose, and the matte versions of the black and silver. The subscription costs $5.99/month (or $69.99/year, which is only a $2 savings), and the Oura is basically useless without the subscription.

Here's how the cost works out on an annual basis:

Oura Ring 5 in black or silver: $399 + $5.99/month subscription = $470.88 for one year, $542.76 for two years

Oura Ring 5 in other colors: $499 + $5.99/month subscription = $570.88 for one year, $642.76 for two years.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is $479 for all colors, and there is no subscription for basic use of the ring. But you can't necessarily stop there, because the Ultrahuman app includes “PowerPlugs” that will give you extra features or analysis screens. Some are totally free, including the caffeine window,  smart alarms, a new parent mode, and a limited version of the cycle and ovulation tracker, but others carry a monthly fee. And if you consider all the optional subscription fees for different PowerPlugs, they can quickly add up:

HealthEx, to connect medical records: $4.99/month

Most people probably wouldn't choose all of them, but even if you just wanted, say, respiratory health and cycle & ovulation pro, you’d quickly outstrip the price of an Oura Ring’s subscription. On the other hand, Ultrahuman also offers an Ultrahuman Max plan for $9.99/month or $99.99/year that includes all the PowerPlugs mentioned above, plus the Les Mills workouts that normally run $11.99/month. That's cheaper than subscribing to all of the options individually, but it will also make the Ultrahuman Ring Pro more expensive than the Oura Ring 5: $578.99 total for one year, or $678.98 for two years. In short, if you want everything that each ring has to offer, the Ultrahuman will cost you more.

Here's the big caveat: I wouldn't recommend bothering with most of the PowerPlugs. For example, "UltraSync for Tesla" recommends settings for your car based on how rested you are, which will be useless if you don't have a Tesla, and probably even if you do. "Cardio adaptability" measures a metric that Ultrahuman says is subtly different from HRV; Oura doesn't measure this adaptability metric, but it's not clear to me whether it's even worth measuring at all (I'd argue probably not).

Ultrahuman's respiratory health PowerPlug ($3.99/month) records sounds while you sleep, which Oura doesn't do; but Oura reports breathing disturbances based on the ring's data, which Ultrahuman doesn't do. Ultrahuman's feature is more expensive.

Ultrahuman offers a premium version of its cycle tracker for $3.99/month, while Oura has a partnership with Natural Cycles that cost $149.99/year. Either will provide more detailed (and, each company says, more accurate) cycle tracking than the basic tracking each app provides without the extras. Oura's option is more expensive.

Ultrahuman's HealthEx Powerplug ($4.99/month) displays information from your medical records throughout the app; Oura lets you import your medical records for free, but uses them mainly in the Advisor (chatbot) and dedicated areas of the app. Ultrahuman's option is more expensive.

Oura's app gives you scores for your readiness, sleep, and recent activity, and it tracks how stressed you seem to be throughout the day. A message at the top of the main screen gives you advice for what to do that day—for example, scaling back your workouts if you seem to be tired or stressed. Ultrahuman does pretty much the same thing, giving you a "next best action" that changes throughout the day, but tends to stick to predictable themes: get more activity if you've been sitting, and that sort of thing.

Both give detailed breakdowns of the factors that contribute to your scores, and both likely overstate how useful their scores are (you don't actually need to change your workout plans just because you had a less-than-perfect night of sleep). But the apps handle the basics pretty similarly: Both have partners and integrations, and you can book blood tests through either app, if you want to do that for some reason.

Ultrahuman gives you a bit more guidance on circadian rhythms, urging you to get in extra steps during certain times of day, and offering to micromanage your caffeine intake. It has a "longevity" tab that puts your long-term habits in terms of how many years they are supposedly subtracting from (or adding to) your lifespan, including measurable metrics like VO2max and a few things that are more inscrutable, like arterial stiffness.

Oura has a whole tab of "vitals" that it calculates from your day-to-day data, which I find more useful than Ultrahuman's data views. The items here include "resilience," which compares your stress to your recovery; a "symptom radar" that can sometimes flag when you're sick; and metrics of sleep regularity and how you're breathing. And, of course, you can check your "cardiovascular age" to see how much younger (or older) you should feel.

Overall, I prefer Oura's approach because the metrics make more sense, are easier to find, and are less likely to feel like they're going way out on a limb relative to the underlying science. Ultrahuman wants you to feel like a cutting-edge biohacker; Oura does a bit more to keep things down to earth. It is a bit funny to remember that both apps, and their wealth of data, are basically just pulling from heart rate readings throughout the day and night. Neither app gives you any truly important information the other doesn't, but Oura's makes more sense to me.

#3370. iPadOS 27.2 adds convenient new multitasking option on iPad

iPadOS 27.2 launched last week with a variety of new features for iPad, including a convenient change for multitasking.

When iPhone Duo first got into users’ hands, several reviews mentioned how the new Split View system felt more intuitive than iPadOS multitasking ever has.

And in iPadOS 27.2, there’s a convenient new multitasking change that’s likely inspired by iPhone Duo.

Apple hasn’t brought over the entire iOS system to the iPad. But it has made one common multitasking feature easier to set up: Split View.

From the official iPadOS 27.2 release notes:

Side-by-side multitasking is easier to set up with the option to choose a second app whenever you tile apps to the left or right with the window controls or menu bar

Starting with iPadOS 26 last year, setting up two apps side-by-side could fairly cumbersome.

You needed to open the first app, resize it, then swipe up from the bottom of the screen to see your other apps, select one, and in many cases manually resize the second app too.

But in iPadOS 27.2, any time you use Apple’s window resizing controls to tile an app left or right, you’ll immediately see the Home Screen and be able to tile a second app with a single tap.

FTA: "Once you master the built-in keyboard shortcuts for app tiling, it becomes even quicker and easier to set up your apps side-by-side."

It’s not identical to the iPhone Duo experience, but it’s a lot closer to it than the old system was.

Once you master the built-in keyboard shortcuts for app tiling, it becomes even quicker and easier to set up your apps side-by-side.

How to improve auto activity tracking on the Fitbit Edge and Fitbit Air

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I just reviewed the Fitbit Edge and the Fitbit Air, and they are easily two of the best fitness trackers of 2026, and devices I’ll likely be recommending for the foreseeable future.

However, one key criticism I had for both: Unreliable auto workout detection. Less of an issue for the screen-sporting Fitbit Edge than the screen-free Fitbit Air, I was hopeful Google would be quick to address this complaint with a firmware update.

And sure enough, the Mountain View Mammoth did just that, announcing improvements to Automatic Activity Detection not just for the latest Fitbits but also the Pixel Watch 5 and older Pixel Watch models.

The update expands the list of trackable activities from just a handful, like walking and bike riding, to over 100, with lots of popular and nuanced exercises covered.

However, even without the latest firmware, there's a quick and easy way to improve auto activity tracking on the Fitbit Air and Fitbit Edge that's buried within the menus of the Google Health app.

This fix addresses one of the two key conditions needed for workout tracking to kick in. You see, Google wearables, by default, require a sustained heart rate and a minimum workout duration of 15 minutes for auto-detection to work.

However, users can manually lower the minimum duration to ten minutes, a change I've found tends to make auto-detection more reliable than the default settings. Here's how to change it.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Read on to see full illustrated instructions for each step.

To improve auto activity tracking on the Fitbit Edge, Fitbit Air, or Pixel Watch 5, first, open the Google Health app on your smartphone and tap on your profile picture in the top right corner of the screen.

Next, scroll down and tap on "Google Health Settings," and then scroll down and tap on "Activity" under the "Preferences" banner.

Once on the Activity page, scroll down and tap on "Activity Detection" near the bottom of the page under the 'Feature settings' banner.

On the Activity Detection page, go ahead and tap on one of the listed activities, like "Walk" or "Bike." Next, tap on "Minimum Duration" to adjust it to a shorter threshold.

Change the minimum duration threshold from the default to 10 minutes by swiping up or down on the options shown.

Finally, with the duration changed to 10 minutes, tap on "Save" and then the back button in the upper left to adjust the minimum duration for other workout types.

I recommend changing the workout duration to ten minutes — the minimum — for all of the activities listed, including walking, biking, and “All other workouts.” Unfortunately, when it comes to “Sports” workouts, the default duration of 15 minutes is the shortest option.

It’s also worth noting that users can revisit a mislabeled activity in the Google Health app and manually correct the workout type. Moreover, the more activities you log on your Fitbit or Pixel Watch, the better your device should get at auto-detecting your favorites.

Finally, keep in mind that auto-detected activities can take up to 30 minutes before appearing in the Google Health app.

#3368. ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: Oscar Winner Takashi Yamazaki’s Vision Of Japan’s Most Iconic Monster Is Back Bigger Than Ever Battling An Even Deadlier Foe

With 2023’s monster hit Godzilla Minus One, Takashi Yamazaki became only the second director after Stanley Kubrick and 2001: A Space Odyssey to take home the Visual Effects Academy Award, and his film became the only Godzilla movie in 70 years to win an Oscar.

Naturally, that all calls for a sequel, doesn’t it? The filmmaker wasn’t sure since he didn’t want to disappoint the legions of fans of the first film, a Japanese Kaiju cinema masterpiece which, unlike most of the Godzilla films, really succeeded in part because of the emotional human story it also had to tell. Well, it is nice to say he hasn’t forgotten that aspect, even as Godzilla Minus Zero, set two years after the first, has gone much bigger and was “filmed for IMAX”. The fabulous Scope visual palette is still there but adding the IMAX brand turns out to complement it rather than smother it.

The irony here is the titular star, Godzilla, is really just a supporting player in his own movie. This one, for much of the 135-minute running time, is more obsessed with another Kaiju, the regally named King Ghidorah (one of my favorite Godzilla foes ever). Ghidorah, in the wake of the apparent death of Godzilla in Minus One, is ruling the skies over Matsumoto, a truly terrifying creature who proves three heads are better than one. He seems invincible but the head of the Large Scale Disaster Response Bureau, Kenju Noda (Hidetake Yoshioka) is convinced he can be banished through electrocution and sets the plan in motion with associates, including Weather whiz and meteorologist Masami Nagasawa (Makoto Aoyama), and Professor Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka), a survivor of unspeakable horrors including the atom bomb dropped on Hiroshima by the Americans to end WWII. The U.S. Army is around too, but with their own motivations, just as Murakami has his. The film’s first half is all about Ghidorah, and also the returning Shikishima family who so movingly figured in Minus One. Watch on Deadline

Koichi Shikishima (Ryunosuki Kamiki) is now married to Noriko (Minami Hamabe), sporting an eye patch and her own secrets, the parents of now five-year-old Akiko (played again by Sae Nagatani). Koichi is happy to put his past as a kamakazi pilot behind him, although still riddled with guilt over still being alive. Noriko’s connection to Godzilla will soon thrust this loving family into crisis as they are drawn into the new disaster when it becomes clear Godzilla is still around, and actually needed by the powers that be to destroy Ghidorah, a complicated plan concocted when all else fails. How the hell do they lure Godzilla out of hiding and to cooperate in this ambitious scheme. This all leads to the film’s truly spectacular Kaiju battle for the ages. Yamazaki had only 35 artisans on board for the equally thrilling fights in Godzilla Minus One, and here only really adds a handful, who all contribute to the remarkable visual effects on display, at an ounce of the cost of major studio productions on this scale. I smell another Oscar.

Still despite all the histrionics on display, it is the human element that makes this a step above the usual monster mashups. In a heartbreaking Solomon-style moment, circumstances force the parents to give up Akiko to an orphanage as their duty to country (and I won’t give the exact details of that but it is pretty persuasive) trumps duty to family. The separation scene is gut wrenching as Akiko fails to understand why she is being abandoned and gives one wail of a goodbye scene.

The craft of Godzilla Minus Zero is stunning to say the least and if ever there was a reason to head out to the local IMAX, this movie gives you one. The good news is this may not be the last of Yamazaki’s dance with Godzilla as the ending leaves room for a third edition, which considering the artistic and crowd- pleasing success of the first two is something to look forward to.

Producer is Kazuaki Kishida. In Japanese with English subtitles.

Title: Godzilla Minus ZeroDistributor: Toho/G KidsRelease Date: November 6, 2026Director/Screenwriter/VFX: Takashi YamazakiCast: Ryunosuki Kamiki, Minami Hamabe, Mio Tanaka, Min Tanaka, Hidetaka Yoshioka, Sae Nagtani, Makoto Aoyama.Rating: RRunning Time: 2 hrs 15 mins

#3367. New report on ‘HomeView Ultra’ product covers features, pricing, more

Apple’s new HomeView product arrives in users’ homes next week, but today a report from The Information outlines what to expect from a larger, high-end ‘HomeView Ultra’ product coming next year.

Today Aaron Tilley at The Information published a report on a forthcoming HomeView product that could be dubbed ‘HomeView Ultra.’

Similar to Mark Gurman’s extensive reporting, Tilley classifies the new home product as a robotics project. He says, “Apple’s new CEO John Ternus wants the company to get serious about robots.”

Per the report, the HomeView Ultra product has “a nine-inch screen that swivels around on an arm and resembles the Pixar lamp.” Tilley writes:

Apple initially began working on the robot in 2019—code-naming it J595—and had modest ambitions for it, envisioning it mostly as a device for video calls. Its robotic arm was intended to allow it to follow someone wherever they were in a room. But hopes for the robot ballooned once Apple executives began wanting to add AI capabilities to it.

The current design for the robot envisions it using a camera and sensors to be fully aware of its environment and act autonomously, allowing it to turn on the lights when someone walks into a room—or perhaps even try to tell a cat to get oﬀ a table. It is meant to be smart enough to avoid accidentally hitting objects around it.

The report notes that much of the hardware for the product “has been finished for around two years.” Software, however, is keeping the device from shipping. This is due to a more ambitious slate of AI-powered features than was originally envisioned.

Pricing is expected to be “around $1,000” per the report, but it may cost more depending on market prices for components. Tilley spoke to several former employees who said they expect Apple to use ‘HomeView Ultra’ branding for the product. As we’ve seen this fall though, Apple has been hesitant to expand its slate of Ultra products.

As for release timing, Tilley says that “Apple hopes to launch the robot next year. It could push the launch out to 2028 though.”

#3366. Bob Dylan Meets With Pope Leo XIV in a Private Audience

Pope Leo XIV has made time for several revered musicians this past year, including Patti Smith and Bad Bunny. On Wednesday, he also held a private audience with Bob Dylan.

His Holiness showcased his fondness for the revered songwriter in his book, Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift, in a citation. The pope quoted Dylan’s unpublished 1963 protest song “Go Away You Bomb” in the book. “‘I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned an’ man-handled,’” the pope quoted from Dylan. The previously unreleased song’s lyrics, which were typewritten and then corrected by hand, were auctioned by Christie’s in the summer of 2013.

It was written by Dylan in 1963 for Izzy Young of the Greenwich Village Folklore Center. “I asked everyone I knew to write a song about the nuclear bomb,” Young told Rolling Stone in 2013. “Bob Dylan came in literally the next day and handed this to me.”

In the pope’s book, he quoted Dylan’s “Go Away You Bomb” and also commended pacifist Dorothy Day for her work for peace.

According to Vatican News, the pair’s meeting on Wednesday was “brief” and consisted of “greetings and a few lighthearted exchanges.” The pair exchanged gifts: The pope presented Dylan a rosary and Dylan gave the pope his autobiography, Chronicles: Volume One.

In June, Pope Leo met with Bad Bunny and others while both were touring Spain. “If they are confronted with the question do they want to see Bad Bunny or do they want to see the pope, I think many will see Bad Bunny,” Leo acknowledged of the musician’s popularity. “But I think there will also be a few here to see the pope. And that says something.”

Fellow Chicagoan Patti Smith met with Pope Leo in August. “This is a moment that shall forever produce a smile,” Smith wrote on Instagram of the encounter at the time. #3365. Five Creative Ways to Spend Your FSA Funds Before the End of the Year

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), you know the drill: Use the funds before the end of the year, or lose them. Unfortunately, chances are slim you can pack the rest of the year with doctor's appointments. Does that mean your hard-earned funds go to waste? Definitely not. You can spend your remaining FSA funds on other qualifying healthcare costs. And what counts as "qualifying" might surprise you—for instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch.

As the end of the year approaches, here are all the ways you can spend any leftover money in your FSA balance.

Many over-the-counter medications and health items are FSA-eligible, including pain relievers, cold medicine, bandages, dental care products, menstrual products, and more. Scan your medicine cabinet and make a list of anything you need to stock up on.

FSA/HSA eligibility for smartwatches and other fitness wearables is real, but the main “catch" (as I’ve previously explained) is proving the device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN).

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. Similarly, smartwatches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does, as long as you can link a relevant documented health concern. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches.

If you want to get creative with it, the official FSA store lets you filter by "surprisingly eligible." Similar to the section above, for some of these items, you'll want to brush up on how exactly to get an LMN to justify certain tech as FSA-eligible for you personally. In the meantime, go crazy and snag yourself Epsom salt for $8.99, Supergoop! sunscreen for $38.00, or perhaps a snazzy massage gun for $349.99.

Knee braces, wrist splints, compression socks, and other orthopedic items can help relieve chronic pain issues. Rather than wait for these issues to rear their heads down the line, use FSA money to offset the costs of these fixes now. If you use eyeglasses or contacts, consider using your FSA dollars to update or refresh your prescriptions. Don't forget to stock up on eye drops and lens solution, too.

If you have medical procedures scheduled for early next year, many healthcare providers will allow you to pre-pay the estimated costs this calendar year using FSA funds. This includes dental work, physical therapy, chiropractic visits, Lasik eye surgery, and more.

However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste. After all, it came out of your paycheck. Check in with your employer’s rules for any balance remaining on Dec. 31 this year, so you aren’t left forfeiting your hard-earned funds. You can find a complete list at the FSA store here.

Use Google Flights to score cheaper holiday airfare

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Booking flights often feels like a game designed for you to lose, with fluctuating algorithms, sneaky add-on fees, and airline websites that push expensive fares by default. Google Flights levels the playing field, but only if you know where to look.

Once you're on the site, the real savings come down to three simple moves: browsing without a locked destination, reading the color-coded calendar, and flipping past curated recommendations to lock in the absolute lowest price.

If your destination is non-negotiable but your dates have a little wiggle room, never book off the first search result. Click directly onto the departure date field to open the full monthly calendar view.

Google automatically scans fares across several months and highlights the cheapest departure and return days in bright green. Shifting your flight forward or back by just 24 hours can routinely cut fares in half, particularly by avoiding popular Thursday and Sunday travel surges in favor of off-peak Tuesdays and Wednesdays.

When your flight list first populates, Google naturally sorts your options under a "Best departing flights" banner. While convenient, this list is a curated compromise: Google prioritizes shorter layovers and reputable mainline carriers over raw savings.

Look just above the top flight card for the Cheapest tab. Switching to this tab strips away those convenience filters, exposing rock-bottom fares from budget airlines, longer self-transfer layovers, and third-party booking agents that frequently undercut direct airline pricing.

Airfare prices fluctuate constantly based on seasonal demand, fuel hedging, and seat inventory. If you are planning a trip several months out, do not panic-buy early.

On your route’s search results page, toggle the Track prices switch on. Google will monitor fare movements in the background and ping your inbox the moment prices drop significantly, ensuring you buy at the bottom of the curve rather than during an artificial peak.

Carol Potter, who played Cindy Walsh, the mom of twins Brenda and Brandon Walsh in the Fox series, will also be featured in the microdrama.

Other shows on the vertical streaming app include Finding Hope (reuniting Fuller House favorites Jodie Sweetin, John Brotherton, and Marla Sokoloff alongside Richard Karn) and Chonda (starring Chonda Pierce and Regan Burns), which broke ground as the vertical microseries format’s first multicam sitcom.

Based in Los Angeles, vertTV continues to elevate mobile entertainment by pairing traditional L.A. production infrastructure, experienced local crews, and veteran Hollywood screenwriters with fast-paced vertical storytelling. Powered by human intelligence, the studio remains deeply committed to authentic artistry, shooting every series with real actors on real sets without the use of generative AI.

Vertical microdramas continue to gain traction as they meet viewers where they spend most of their time on — mobile phones. #3361. These 10 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple dropped the first developer beta for iOS 27.3 on Tuesday. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

#3359. ‘This Had Better Work’: Why This Folk-Country Band Sold Their House to Go on Tour

There’s committing yourself to a life of music, and then there’s selling your house, buying a van, and hitting the road. The Minnesota folk trio Wild Horses threw themselves into the latter.

In 2021, the band got booked at the Grand Rapids Riverfest, a regional end-of-summer festival that has featured headliners like Jason Isbell and Wilco. Bolstered by the high-profile slot, Jed LaPlant and his partner Ariana, the husband-and-wife songwriters who founded Wild Horses, sold their home, picked up a 1989 Chevy Astro van, and hit the road.

“We decided this is what we’re gonna do,” Jed says. “We’re going all-in.”

Since then, they’ve spent nearly all their time on tour, playing their own gigs and supporting headliners like Charley Crockett, Trampled by Turtles, and Sam Barber. The LaPlants found that such a nomadic life was the perfect catalyst for songwriting. “Whatever it is — roots or Americana music — is unique, in that the job of it fuels the inspiration,” Jed says, recalling something a peer once told him. “Being out on the road is the fuel.”

Wild Horses took their road experiences and assembled them for The In Between, the group’s second studio album, released in October via Outlaw Foundry/Atlantic Outpost. It’s an autobiographical snapshot of a grassroots folk band trying to navigate an era when selling all your belongings and pursuing a music career sounds, at best, ill-advised.

After releasing their debut album, Runaway, in 2022, Wild Horses upgraded from that Astro Van to a high-miles coach and converted it into a tour bus. The early lineup fluctuated between four and six players — including banjo and trumpet — before they found a path ahead as a trio with bassist Landon Pahl. A longtime friend of Jed’s, Pahl followed his pal’s lead and quit his day job, joining the LaPlants for a life on the bus.

On The In Between, Wild Horses —Jed on vocals and guitar; Ariana on vocals, fiddle, and keys; and Pahl on bass — compile nine tracks, each of them written by the LaPlants. Early single “Sunrise on the Absaroke” gives the album its title. It’s a road-weary tune about making ends meet in close quarters and includes the line, “Livin’ in the in between, trying to beat the desert heat/there’s nothing I could do to keep from crying my way home.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

On “Take It As It Comes,” which plays out over a high-tempo guitar-and-fiddle melody that evokes horses galloping, the LaPlants double down on their life on the run. “There’s a sense of urgency in that song,” Jed says, “that I think came out of playing a lot of really noisy bars in places where we really didn’t belong — trying to win over people. That urgency came from the idea that this had better work.”

Grand Rapids is a town of a little more than 11,000 in north-central Minnesota, named for the rapids of the far northern reaches of the Mississippi River that cuts through downtown. The LaPlants met in town, playing open-mic nights, and fell in love.

“We were both working other jobs,” Jed says. “We were paying for a house and all that. Then, during Covid, I ended up with a broken back, and the construction job I had wasn’t gonna cut it. We were at a crossroads. We started jamming with friends of ours — a bass player and a drummer in town here — just to keep out the cold.”

So far, it’s working. The band have found receptive audiences on the road, especially during an October tour with Trampled by Turtles. In December, they’ll join Sam Barber for a swing that begins in the Midwest and ends on the West Coast.

Jed has a personal goal of understanding how people connect with his songs, and spending time playing before Barber or Crockett allows him the chance to witness firsthand what lyric or melody is moving the needle. Trending Stories Trump's Bizarre Journey Through the Stages of Grief as Democrats Dominated the Midterms Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner Did an AMA About That Shower Scene, His Sniffing, and ‘You Can See Everything’ Dane Cook’s Brother Robbed Him Blind. Now He’s Rebuilding His Life — And Gunning for a Comeback Trump Is Already Crying That He’s Not to Blame for Republican Wipeout

“It’s satisfying when you have moments where you can see people crying along with moments that came out of the grief of tearing down our dream house,” he says. “Then equally, seeing the joy on people’s faces when we get to those moments where the music climbs and builds.”

Josh Crutchmer is a journalist and author whose upcoming book, Sonoran Sounds, is set for release in March 2027 via Back Lounge Publishing.

#3358. Political Ad Revenue Breaks Record For Sinclair, Lifting It To Better-Than-Expected Q3 Results

Sinclair cashed in on political advertising during the third quarter even before the “blue tsunami” officially reached shore. The broadcaster rode a 55% gain in the category compared with the previous midterm election in 2022 to post better-than-expected financial results.

The company said it sold $136 million in political ads during the July-to-September period, with the spending hitting an all-time record of $455 million in all of 2026, ahead even of the 2024 presidential haul of $405 million. The company’s previous full-year high for a midterm cycle was $333 million in 2022.

Total revenue increased 16% from the prior-year quarter, hitting $893 million. Adjusted EBITDA more than doubled to $213 million, with earnings per share of 60 cents swinging to the black after a 2-cents-per-share loss a year earlier. Watch on Deadline

CEO Chris Ripley said more quarterly results are yet to be reported by rival companies, but it appeared that local TV stations as a sector maintained market share levels from prior political cycles. With live sports continuing to pace the overall linear landscape, some political campaigns opted for national broadcast buys rather than local stations, given the comparative expense profiles. That created the odd spectacle of East Coast sports fans being served PAC-funded spots backing Senate candidates in Texas or Iowa.

In 2015 and 2016, as Donald Trump was rising to dominance, Sinclair played a key role in his unforeseen triumph over Hillary Clinton. At the time, Sinclair was also known for more expressly right-of-center programming and “must-run” editorials. A decade later, and in the wake of Democrats’ stinging rebuke of Trump in the midterms, the climate has shifted. Still, Sinclair remains one of the primary local players, though it is now No. 2 station behind market leader Nexstar.

Third-party war chests, including nearly half a billion from Elon Musk, paced the record spending levels. The amount of ad spending did not always correlate to the result, however. Texas Gov.-Elect Gina Hinojosa soundly defeated incumbent Greg Abbott despite him outspending her by a roughly 10-to-1 margin.

Rob Weisbord, COO and president of local media for Sinclair, told Wall Street analysts on the company’s earnings call that the political haul this year “bodes well for the upcoming 2028 election cycle, which will be here before we know it. Notably, 2028 will present a dual open primary for both parties, for the presidential nominations. So we expect early and aggressive spending as both parties will want to introduce themselves nationally. While our footprint is well positioned throughout many battleground states, we also believe that the entire broadcast sector did well during the election cycle.”

He added that management commentary at rival companies as well as industry forecasts provide evidence “of local broadcast television being a key delivery platform of political advertising.”

#3354. The Votes Are In: Americans Don’t Want Data Centers

Democrats won big in Tuesday’s midterms, not only taking back the House of Representatives and Senate by overwhelming margins, but rebuking Republican candidates down the entire ticket in deep-red states like Texas, Mississippi, and Tennessee. Pundits and politicians are offering plenty of explanations for it — the exorbitant cost of living, the war in Iran, Republican candidates simply not being good enough — but there may be another thing that drove voters to the polls: the public’s deep distrust of AI data centers going up across the nation.

According to the report Data Centers on the 2026 Ballot, published by the firm Redbud Consulting, which has been tracking the initiatives, the election showed a decisive loss for data centers. Since yes and no could mean different things depending on the ballot, Redbud broke it down by votes to “restrict” or “allow” data centers in their analysis. Of the 39 nationwide referendums that have been fully counted, 38 of them enacted new restrictions for potential new data centers.

“For as much as Republicans did poorly last night, the one thing that did even worse were data centers,” says Alex Lundry, founder and CEO of Redbud Consulting. “For the most part, the restrict side has gotten about 77 percent of the vote in each of these races.” This lines up with recent polling: On Monday, Gallup published a survey that showed 70 percent of Americans don’t want data centers near where they live.

The one initiative that didn’t pass so far, Lundry notes, was in the town of Harwood, North Dakota, where an initiative would have imposed “additional significant requirements” on “certain development or building projects within the City.” Though the measure was ostensibly there to target data centers, Lundry notes that the phrase “data center” wasn’t itself present in the ballot language, which could have affected its outcome. “To be clear, there are literally only, what, 430 people voting on this issue in the city of Harwood,” he says. “So it’s hard to read too much into this, but it is interesting.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

According to Lundry’s analysis, those that used the phrase data center had stronger support, but most still managed to pass. In Ohio, for example, 21 separate local initiatives used largely the same language, calling for a mandatory referendum process on the construction of any structure that “occupies 50 or more contiguous acres, draws more than 20 megawatts of electrical power at peak capacity, or consumes more than 500,000 gallons of water per day.” All 21 of those ballot measures passed.  Trending Stories Trump's Bizarre Journey Through the Stages of Grief as Democrats Dominated the Midterms Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner Did an AMA About That Shower Scene, His Sniffing, and ‘You Can See Everything’ Dane Cook’s Brother Robbed Him Blind. Now He’s Rebuilding His Life — And Gunning for a Comeback Trump Is Already Crying That He’s Not to Blame for Republican Wipeout

Aside from the ballot initiatives specifically targeting the construction of data centers, candidates who campaigned against them also saw huge wins in yesterday’s elections. As journalist Jael Holzman noted in the climate news site Heatmap, Keisha Lance Bottoms and Amy Acton won the governorships in Georgia and Ohio, respectively, thanks in part to their hard-lines against data centers. In New Jersey, Zack Mullock beat Republican representative Jeff Van Drew to win a long-red seat in Cape May, thanks to his repudiation of data centers, while in Virginia, Shannon Taylor did the same to Rep. Rob Wittman.

Elon Musk and Trump’s other tech cronies may have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into the midterms this year, but for now, at least, the democratic process is still strong — and Americans are making it clear where they stand on the issues.

The XM6 headphones improve on what were already excellent headphones. Sony upped the count of microphones from eight to 12 when compared to the XM5, which improves more than just how well you sound to someone on a phone call. The microphones are used in almost all of its features, like ANC, Adaptive Sound Control, and the headphones' Ambient Sound mode. They hear your surroundings to adapt their features accordingly. If you switch from a noisy room to a quiet one, the XM6 can switch from ANC to aware mode (if you have Adaptive Sound Control on).

These headphones have a lot more features that you can nerd out on in their companion app. The audio quality is second to none, with the fully customizable EQ giving you plenty of options to get the sound how you like it. I really like being able to see what codec you're listening to in the app's main menu. That way, there's no guessing if you're getting the best audio quality or not. They will give you 30 hours of battery life with ANC on and 40 hours of juice with ANC off. There's an AUX (3.5mm) jack for wired listening, which is a nice touch for audiophiles who still rock iPod Classics (or is that just me?).

The XM6s were not just the best headphones of 2025, but are still the best ones of 2026 and likely to be the best ones for years to come. For $378, you'll be securing the best for a record-low price.

As Denis Villeneuve prepares to release the conclusion of his Dune trilogy, Timothée Chalamet is praising the ending of the epic saga.

#3350. Cynthia Erivo to Play Tupac Shakur’s Mother in Snoop Dogg Biopic

Cynthia Erivo has been tapped to portray Afeni Shakur, the mother of Tupac Shakur, in the upcoming Universal Pictures biopic about Snoop Dogg, as The Hollywood Reporter reports.

Erivo joins a cast that includes Jonathan Daviss, Myles Bullock, Lauren London, Camron Jones, Algee Smith, Tre Hale, Laya DeLeon Hayes, Olly Sholotan, Corey Champagne, Jonica Booth, and SwayvoTwain.

Afeni Shakur was a former Black Panther and political activist, and was the subject of several of her son’s songs, including the 1995 single “Dear Mama.” A year after the song was released, Tupac was gunned down in Las Vegas and died a week later. Afeni Shakur launched the Tupac Amaru Shakur Foundation one year after her son’s death, and oversaw the late rapper’s estate. She died in 2016 at age 69.

Daviss (Outer Banks) stars as Snoop Dogg and Jones (Panic) stars opposite as Tupac Shakur. SwayvoTwain — the musician born Michael D’Angelo Archer II to late legendary artists D’Angelo and Angie Stone — will portray Notorious B.I.G. in the film. Bullock plays Dr. Dre, Hale stars as Suge Knight, London plays Snoop’s mother Beverly Tate, and Laya DeLeon Hayes as Snoop’s wife, Shante.

The Craig Brewer-directed film is currently in production in California and producers include Snoop Dogg and Death Row Pictures president Sara Ramaker, alongside Imagine Entertainment’s Allan Mandelbaum and Brian Grazer, who was behind Eminem’s 8 Mile. The film is expected to arrive in theaters in August 2027. Gym-goers, Fitness Plus just got a hell of a lot better!

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I’ve been writing about Apple Fitness Plus since it launched in December 2020 — what started as workouts with your favorite trainers has evolved into a much larger ecosystem, and this might be one of its most exciting transformations to date. Today, Apple has announced new Gym Strength plans, launching on Fitness Plus.

These personalized four-week training plans move away from group classes and more towards helping users reach their own fitness goals. The plans are progressive and work with larger commercial gyms, as well as with minimal equipment at home. Let’s dive into everything you can expect from this update:

Gym Strength is designed to take the guesswork out of the gym. You’ll find it in the Fitness Plus menu, and you’ll be asked to answer a few questions before you begin. This helps the algorithm to create a programme best suited to you. You’ll input how familiar you are with strength training, your goal, the areas of your body you want to work, the days of the week you prefer to work out on, and, most importantly, the equipment you have available.

Once you’ve got your plan, you can turn on Apple Intelligence-powered training notes, or leave them off. The note is designed to summarize your progress and give you an overview of how this workout can help you reach your goals.

One of the most difficult things about working out alone is making sure you’re moving with good form. You can move through the Gym Strength workouts at your own pace, with your own music, but each exercise will be demoed by a Fitness Plus trainer to ensure you’re getting the form right. You can tap on the video to expand it and see the trainer from three different angles.

Each exercise has recommended sets, reps, and load, depending on what you’ve lifted before and what you are hoping to achieve. You can easily tap Swap on an exercise if you just don’t want to do it, and swap out the equipment available if you’re in a busy gym and don’t want to wait.

On-screen, you’ll also see a dynamic bar, which shows you at a glance how you’re progressing through your workout.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Of course, this is Apple, so seamless integration is a given. You can see your exercises, reps, and load from your wrist if you’re using an Apple Watch during the workout, as well as what’s coming next.

You can also see your heart rate data and how many calories you’ve burned.

Unlike a strength plan you’ve downloaded from the internet or grabbed from ChatGPT, the Gym Strength plans are designed to progress with you session by session. With input from the Fitness Plus strength trainers, the plans give you an estimated load when suggesting an exercise you’ve not done before. Using your inputs, the plan will tell you when it thinks you need to increase the weight you’re lifting, based on your past performances.

I’ll be grabbing some weights and heading to the gym to test my own Gym Strength plan over the next few weeks. Watch this space!
