#3299. Meet the Anthropic Engineer Keeping Its AI Agent Trustworthy

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

His data systems make sure Claude’s answers are accurate

IEEE Senior Member Gurmeet Saran is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind Claude’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs.

If you’ve ever wondered how Claude and similar AI agents can answer complex questions in seconds and where they get the information, you’re not alone.

Gurmeet Saran works to find that answer every day as an engineer at Anthropic in San Francisco, the AI research company behind Claude. The IEEE senior member is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind the chatbot’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs.

Gurmeet Saran Employer Anthropic in San FranciscoTitle Member of technical staffMember grade IEEE senior memberAlma maters University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India

University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India

Safety is a priority for Anthropic, he says. According to Claude’s mission statement, the company wants the AI agent to be “genuinely helpful to the people it works with or on behalf of, as well as to society, while avoiding actions that are unsafe, unethical, or deceptive.” Crucial to the mission is ensuring that researchers can observe and understand how AI models behave, a challenge that is especially acute for large language models, Saran says.

“We have decent tools to monitor databases and web services,” he says, “but for LLMs, we’re still figuring it out.”

Saran’s interest in computing systems dates back to his childhood in Kolkata, where he logged as much time as he could in the school computer lab.

“I remember the first time I used one of the computers,” he says. “What struck me was that you could write instructions, and the machine would follow them exactly. No ambiguity.

After graduating from high school in 1999, he stayed in India to pursue advanced degrees. He earned a bachelor’s degree in electronics and telecommunication engineering in 2004 at the University of Kalyani. In 2010, he earned a master’s degree in software engineering from the Birla Institute of Technology and Science in Pilani.

While a graduate student, he began his career in 2007 at Yahoo as a technical lead of the data team in Bengaluru, India. While there, he encountered the project that shaped his career trajectory: working on web analytics and business intelligence reporting solutions.

“We kept running into a frustrating problem,” he recalls. “Different teams would calculate the same website metric—something like daily active site users—using slightly different logic, and end up with conflicting answers. It sounds like a small issue, but when leadership is making decisions about resource allocation and product development using that data, not knowing which number is correct becomes a problem.”

The team built a central data repository with defined metrics, essentially serving as a single source of truth. Saran created a model that defined what “daily active site users” means, breaking down which events counted, how to handle edge cases (or when standard code fails), and more.

With the new model, data teams across the company could rely on a standard method to determine the number of daily active users for the projects and sites they were responsible for and obtain comparable results using the same logic.

From there, Saran and his team built Yahoo! Digits, an internal web analytics tool used for all the company’s products.

Saran left Yahoo in 2010 to join Intuit as a staff engineer in Mountain View, Calif. He helped build the analytics infrastructure that unified data across the company’s products, including TurboTax and QuickBooks accounting software. During his tenure, Intuit developed a feature that detected fraudulent tax filings in real time. It required Saran and other engineers to build a system to protect taxpayer data while adhering to strict U.S. Internal Revenue Service policies.

“IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations.”

Saran joined Meta (known as Facebook at the time) in 2016 as a lead software engineer in Menlo Park, Calif. The company was facing controversy over its video metrics: Meta publicly acknowledged an error that caused it to overstate the number of views for posted videos.

“This wasn’t a coding bug; it was an architectural problem,” Saran says. He built a system that worked similarly to what he had developed at Intuit, whereby one single truth was defined to govern all video view metrics across the site.

That system, Metric360, eventually became part of the site’s architecture. By the time he left Meta in 2021, he says, Metric360 was being used across the company to calculate video metrics.

He left the company to become a principal software engineer at Wealthfront, a financial services company in Palo Alto, Calif. He helped build the company’s data infrastructure.

Saran joined Anthropic in 2025 as a member of the technical staff.

To describe the implications of his work, he uses a medical analogy: “Imagine a doctor is monitoring a patient’s vital signs and making treatment decisions based on those numbers. What if one or a few of the medical devices used were slightly miscalibrated? Even if most readings are fine, it’s a serious problem because the difficult decisions happen in the margins.

“It’s the same with AI systems. My job is essentially to make sure the instruments are giving accurate readings—that the data means what it says it means.”

His job comes with high stakes and complex problems to solve.

“AI agents are especially tricky to observe,” he says. “When a system is taking sequences of actions [generating conversational responses with different users], you need a way to capture what it did, what information it was working from, and whether outcomes matched what the end user expected. And you have to do all of that without exposing anyone’s private information—the systems are designed to recognize sensitive data and keep it protected as it flows through. It’s a much more demanding observability problem than anything I’ve worked on before.”

Solving for system reliability while AI is still in its early days of adoption is both Saran’s passion and the problem that keeps him up at night, he says.

“I think making AI systems genuinely auditable and transparent is one of the more important engineering problems of the next decade,” he says, “and it doesn’t get talked about as much as model capabilities do.”

“After more than 20 years of building data infrastructure across organizations like Yahoo, Intuit, Meta, and Wealthfront,” he says, “I wanted to contribute back to the technical community through peer review, publishing, and engaging with the broader engineering research ecosystem.”

He says he believes IEEE can play an essential role in shaping the future of AI through its standards work.

“We have standards for everything, from building codes to software testing,” he says. “AI infrastructure needs something similar, and IEEE has the credibility and the reach to do that.”

Another problem that IEEE can solve for, he says, is access: “IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters, especially as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations in a few cities.”

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

There’s always something worth watching on Prime Video, but with so many shows competing for a place on the trending list, figuring out what deserves a spot on your watchlist can be tricky. The streamer’s top 10 shows list is actually a handy place to start, but not everything trending is necessarily worth binge-watching. So, I’ve picked out three shows from this week’s rankings that I think are worth your time.

That includes a little something for everyone, whether you’re after a gritty action-thriller now streaming its second season, a crime comedy pairing an unlikely duo with plenty of chemistry, or a lighthearted romantic drama full of unexpected connections. They offer three very different viewing experiences, but each has something that makes it worth adding to your watchlist. Here’s what I’d be checking out this week.

This list is based on the Prime Video U.S. top 10 shows as of Wednesday, November 4, 2026.

Prime Video’s “The Terminal List” is back, and it’s clearly still a hit with viewers, currently sitting at No. 1 on the platform’s charts. Based on Jack Carr’s bestselling military thriller novels, the action-packed series also leans into its psychological drama and the emotional weight that comes with these experiences. After a four-year wait since its 2022 debut, all eight episodes of season 2 are now available to stream, giving fans plenty to get stuck into. If you enjoy shows like “Reacher” and “Tom Clancy’s Jack Ryan,” this should be your next pick.

James Reece (Chris Pratt) is a Navy SEAL commander whose entire platoon is ambushed during a covert mission. After returning home with conflicting memories of what happened, Reece begins investigating the operation and discovers that the people responsible may be closer to home than he ever imagined. As he follows a trail of evidence, he finds himself caught up in a far-reaching government conspiracy. Season 2 picks up after Reece completes his revenge mission, following him as he’s drawn into a new operation involving the CIA, a former ally and a resurgent Al-Qaeda network.

Fancy something a little lighter after all the action and drama? “Wild Cards” is a fun crime series that should be right up your alley if you enjoyed shows like “Psych,” “White Collar” or “Castle.” It has witty banter and an entertaining central partnership with plenty of episodic mysteries, making it an easy show to dip in and out of. All 10 episodes of season 3 are now available on Prime Video, so you can catch up at your own pace without needing to buy individual episodes or sign up for an extra subscription. It’s a great choice when you want something entertaining.

“Wild Cards” follows the unlikely partnership between demoted detective Cole Ellis (Giacomo Gianniotti) and clever con artist Max Mitchell (Vanessa Morgan). After Max is arrested and helps Ellis solve a local case, the pair are offered a chance to turn things around. The catch is that they have to work together, with Ellis relying on traditional police work and Max using her talent for disguises, elaborate schemes and talking her way into almost any situation. As they investigate a new case each week, the two gradually learn how to work as a team, despite their very different approaches to solving crimes.

“Love in Disguise” is a fun South Korean series that puts a fresh spin on the romantic comedy formula by adding a little mystery and suspense. Based on the popular Kakao web novel, the show brings together the playful chaos of a gender-swap rom-com with the twists of a corporate thriller. It’s a slightly different take on the K-drama formula, giving viewers plenty of romantic complications alongside a more suspenseful storyline. If you enjoy Korean dramas that offer romance, comedy and a few unexpected twists, this one is worth checking out.

Kang Jae-hee (Seol In-ah) is a former special forces officer turned detective who goes undercover to investigate Yoon Yi-jun (Yim Si-wan), the wealthy heir to a powerful business empire and the prime suspect in his secretary’s murder. To get close to him and uncover evidence, Jae-hee disguises herself as a man and takes a job as his personal secretary. However, keeping her real identity under wraps isn’t easy, especially as Yi-jun becomes increasingly suspicious of his new employee. As the investigation progresses, their complicated working relationship takes some unexpected turns.

#3296. Adobe puts its marketing AI agent inside ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot

Adobe’s CX Enterprise Coworker now plugs into the AI tools marketers already use. New MCP connectors also link it to Amazon Ads, Demandbase, Meta campaigns and Snowflake.

Adobe’s AI agent for marketing teams now works inside ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot and Databricks Genie, the company said on Wednesday. Adobe expects Amazon Quick, IBM and Snowflake to follow soon.

The agent, CX Enterprise Coworker, plans and runs customer experience work across Adobe’s marketing software. In ChatGPT, it comes as a plugin. Adobe made the agent generally available in June.

Adobe says the agent tracks campaign results and trends. It also forecasts audiences, improves customer journeys and helps with planning and project management. It runs with human oversight. It is built on two open standards for AI agents: the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent2Agent (A2A).

Anjul Bhambhri leads engineering for the product at Adobe.

“Today, marketers often use AI tools in isolation, without the organizational context and domain intelligence needed to personalize every stage of the customer lifecycle,” Bhambhri said.

Adobe also launched connectors that link the agent to other companies’ systems through ready-made MCP servers. Partners include Amazon Ads, Demandbase, Microsoft Work IQ, RainFocus and Snowflake. There is also a connector for Meta ad campaigns. Marketers can then pull data and take actions across several systems with a single request, Adobe said.

Consulting firms including Accenture, Deloitte Digital, EY, IBM and PwC are building industry-specific versions of the agent. Agencies such as dentsu, Havas, Omnicom, Publicis and WPP also add their own tools to it.

Rob Howard runs Copilot’s platform and extensibility work at Microsoft.

“This gives marketing teams the speed and flexibility to orchestrate more personalized experiences at scale,” Howard said.

Adobe says more than 20,000 brands use its software for content, customer engagement and brand visibility. In August, it put its creative tools inside ChatGPT. It has also signed agentic AI deals with Jet2 for holidays and Heathrow’s new website.

#3295. IEEE Continues Preparations for the Realignment of Its Regions

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

The redrawn IEEE region map that will become effective in 2028.

Progress continues in restructuring IEEE’s geographic regions, as outlined in The Institute’s February 2023 article “IEEE Is Realigning Its Geographic Regions.”

The restructuring is defined in the image of the redrawn map in this article.

Although the new regional alignment will not officially take place until 1 January 2028, several activities have begun within IEEE Member and Geographic Activities (MGA) and across other IEEE organizational units. Within MGA, volunteers and staff have been actively addressing system enhancements, director/director-elect elections, governance updates, communications, and regional finances and offerings.

Work will continue from now until the effective date of realignment in 2028. The change will not affect your IEEE membership, nor will it change either your local IEEE section or chapter.

If you have any questions regarding the realignment, contact Reg-Realignment@ieee.org.

IEEE Member and Geographic Activities oversees IEEE membership and the activities of its geographic units worldwide.

#3294. Apple earnings suggest the iPhone 18 launch strategy is really working

Yesterday’s AAPL earnings report revealed record revenue for a September quarter, and within it was an arguably even more significant record: iPhone revenue.

That’s because this year’s quarter only includes just two new iPhone models compared to the four released last year …

Apple reported fiscal quarter four revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12% year on year. Within that was iPhone revenue of $57.58 billion, which was also a quarterly record. What makes this significant is the year-on-year comparison, when you consider the new iPhone launch revenue included within each quarter.

(Although the iPhone Duo was announced at the same time, pre-orders didn’t open until October, so none of this revenue is included in Apple’s fiscal Q4.)

The main thing that changed this year is that Apple didn’t launch a base model iPhone 18 alongside the Pro models: that launch won’t happen until early next year. The biggest factor in this decision was likely component shortages, Apple wanting to ensure that it could fulfill demand for premium models, but the revenue figures suggest that the timings also influenced purchase decisions.

Many people upgrade their iPhones on a fixed cycle, be that every one, two, or three years – and that cycle begins each September. When upgrade time rolled around and there was no base model iPhone 18 available, it seems likely that a significant number of those who would have bought it decided to instead opt for the iPhone 18 Pro rather than wait.

That may suggest rather modest sales of the base model iPhone 18 when it rolls around, but if Apple managed to persuade a significant number of would-be buyers to opt for a more expensive model, the company won’t be shedding any tears about that.

Of course, there are a couple of other factors in the mix here. First, the iPhone 17 proved extremely popular and remains on sale today, so it will have contributed something to this year’s Q4 revenue. Second, Apple cited revenue rather than profit, and the $100 price increase for this year’s Pro models will played a role. But overall I do think it paints a very encouraging picture for this split launch strategy.

What’s your take? Do you think it reflects well on iPhone 18 Pro sales, or do you think it can be explained away by the price increase and continuing popularity of the iPhone 17? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

#3293. Apple CEO John Ternus criticized for ‘scripted’ approach to first earnings call

Investors didn’t seem overly happy about yesterday’s Apple earnings call despite the record results. That likely reflects the company’s cautious take on margins in the current quarter, but some have also criticized what they describe as a very “scripted” approach by new CEO John Ternus.

Bloomberg was the biggest critic, describing it as a “timid” performance that left analysts “sorely disappointed” …

Apple investors and fans hoping to get an insight into the philosophy of new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus on Monday were left sorely disappointed. The 51-year-old’s first earnings call was a timid affair, with Ternus taking cover behind a carefully written script as analysts peppered him with questions.

Newly minted CEO plays it safe during his first high-stakes earnings call? Absolutely shocking! Seriously, what did Bloomberg expect?

Lee acknowledged that the slump in pre-market trading will have been largely driven by Apple’s caution about rising expenses in the current quarter. The company said that memory costs were continuing to rise and that building out Siri AI data centers we’re going to add to the RAM bill. But he argued that Ternus missed an opportunity to talk up the company.

In front of Ternus on Monday night was a chance to counteract the gloom and doom by instilling in Wall Street the fundamentals of the Ternus Doctrine — what he sees Apple becoming under his tenure, the “product guy” taking the company to a new era of innovation. Instead, he spoke like a man glancing at the clock and wishing the minutes away.

Fortune’s Sebastian Herrera was less vocal but echoed some of the criticism.

Ternus fielded some questions but also delegated answers to Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh and Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan, who Apple said would participate in earnings calls moving forward, something the company hasn’t done for years. Ternus projected confidence on the call, but he appeared to stick mostly to scripted marketing points.

It will of course take Ternus some time to develop his own style when it comes to all of the varied aspects of the role, including addressing analysts in earnings calls, but I thought he took a measured but optimistic approach. Given the famously reticent style of his predecessor, the criticism strikes me as rather odd.

What’s your take? Please share in the comments.

The iPhone Duo adapted iOS 27 for a new form factor but, in the process, got some criticism for the decision to lock the taskbar to the right-hand side. In fact, if you're a leftie and want to use the Duo with a single hand, you've got to use the non-dominant one.

That situation just got a little better with the arrival of the iOS 27.3 developer beta this week. The update brings Reachability to the iPhone Duo, allowing users to move the content within reach, just as you can on a candybar iPhone.

Only instead of shifting the content from the top down, the Duo will now let users swipe left from the left or right from the right edge of the screen to bring it within striking distance of your preferred thumb.

For left-handed users, it's a step in the right direction, and it will work on both the 5.4-inch outer display and the 7.6-inch nano-textured inner display.

Reachability will be turned on by default once the software update is installed, but if you want to find it yourself, head to Settings > Accessibility > Reachability.

Alongside bringing Reachability to the Duo, 27.3 will also give Siri AI a much bigger playground to explore across iOS, macOS, iPadOS and visionOS. The upgraded assistant will now work inside Music, Messages, Photos, Calendar and Reminders, letting users, for example, ask it to build a specific playlist in Apple Music or create Calendar events.

Going further, Apple is also opening Siri AI's capabilities up to third-party developers via App Intents. Essentially, this could make good on the promise years ago that Apple Intelligence would be able to work across a user's apps to build a personal context.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

Back in 2024, then-CEO Tim Cook laid out what set Apple's AI plans apart: “Our unique approach combines generative AI with a user’s personal context to deliver truly helpful intelligence."

It seems like reality is about to finally caught up to the vision.

"Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more," Apple posted on its developer site.

"So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order. For complex requests, we’re also introducing skills to let you teach Siri AI how to combine several actions into a single experience."

The public release for iOS 27.3 is planned for later this year, at which point we could really see Siri AI start to spread its wings.

#3291. Everything You Should Know About This Year's Black Friday Sales

As is often the case with major sales these days, retailers are increasingly blurring the lines between early deals and the official start of a sale. Black Friday sales appear to be becoming a month-long event, with early deals appearing in the first week of the month. If you haven't been paying attention, major retailers have already put out their plans and even started churning out deals. But you're still in time to make this upcoming Black Friday sale a great one. Here is everything you need to know to prepare you for the big sale.

Black Friday is always the day after Thanksgiving. This year, Black Friday starts at midnight on Nov. 27. Cyber Monday is the Monday following Black Friday, which starts at midnight on Nov. 30.

The major retailers doing sales are the usual: Amazon, Best Buy, Target, Walmart, Home Depot, and many others. Currently, Walmart has publicized its plans already and has early deals available. Best Buy is offering one of the largest Black Friday and Cyber Week sales, with multiple events and early deals. Target has a three-day event. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, use price trackers or refer to guides like our live blog that use price trackers for you, and don’t stress over finding the perfect timing. The “best” deal will always depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers that can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot.

Unlike Spring or Summer sales, Black Friday doesn't focus on specific categories, which means everything is fair game for discounts. In previous years, we've seen tech, tools, fitness equipment, outdoor supplies and furniture, bedding, video games, kitchen appliances, and more. This is one of the best times to make a list of what you need and start tracking prices. You're likely to find what you're looking for discounted, and probably at its lowest price it has ever been. If you'd like to avoid having to do all that work, we always do it for you. Just follow our Black Friday coverage.

The WH-1000XM5 were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (originally $399.99).

The Bose SoundLink Plus hasn’t been on the market for long, but it’s already earned strong reviews—CNET labeled it “the Goldilocks of Bose Bluetooth speakers,” and it’s down to $179 (originally $269).

The all-in-one Eufy E25 robot vacuum and mop has a self-cleaning roller mop, and it is 40% off, reaching $599.98 (originally $999.99). The roller is rinsed with clean water as it mops, then cleaned at the dock, meaning you don't need to spend as much time cleaning it yourself.

Amazon is selling both right now at a $200 discount. That brings the 13-inch MacBook Air to $1,099.99 (down from $1,299) and the 15-inch MacBook Air to $1,299 (originally $1,499), reaching their lowest prices since the June price hikes.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 only launched in September, and it’s already seeing an early Black Friday discount of $100 on Amazon, bringing it down to $699.99 (originally $799).

#3290. New iPad mini hands-on: Refreshed design, OLED display, more

Apple’s smallest iPad has gotten its biggest update in years. The new iPad mini features a much thinner and lighter design, a larger OLED display, water resistance, and the powerful A20 Pro chip.

I’ve been testing the new iPad mini, and there’s a lot to like — but also a couple of frustrations. Here’s everything you need to know.

The new iPad mini lives up to the “mini” name even more than its predecessor. It’s significantly thinner, down from 6.3mm on the previous iPad mini to 5.4mm on the new model. In fact, that puts it very close to the ultra-thin iPad Pro and the unfolded iPhone Duo. Here’s how it compares:

The new iPad mini is also significantly lighter, dropping from 293 grams to 255 grams. That puts it in the realm of the iPhone Duo, for comparison’s sake:

The reduction in weight and thickness was immediately noticeable when I picked up the new iPad mini. It feels significantly nicer to hold, more premium, and less “dense” in my hands.

The new iPad mini features an 8.5-inch screen, a slight increase from the previous generation’s 8.3-inch display. The overall footprint is mostly the same (the new model is actually about 2.2mm narrower). The larger screen is possible because the new iPad mini’s bezels are 24 percent thinner than before.

In addition to allowing a bigger screen in the same form factor, the narrower bezels also modernize the iPad mini’s overall look and feel. The bezels are noticeably slimmer than the iPad Air and base model iPad, and slightly thinner than the iPad Pro.

With smaller bezels, a thinner chassis, and a lighter weight, the new iPad mini feels significantly more premium than before. It reminds me less of the base model iPad or iPad Air and more of the iPad Pro, just shrunken down.

The big news about the display, though, is the switch to OLED. This marks Apple’s first non-Pro iPad to offer an OLED screen. It’s not the fancy tandem OLED display of the iPad Pro, but it’s a huge improvement over the previous model’s LCD panel.

The new iPad mini offers SDR brightness up to 600 nits, up from the previous model’s 500 nits max. The iPad mini also supports HDR content, with up to 1200 nits peak brightness.

The new iPad mini’s screen is undeniably an improvement over its predecessor. All of the inherent benefits of OLED apply here, including better colors, improved contrast, higher brightness, and more.

Unfortunately, the new iPad mini’s screen has one limitation: it doesn’t support ProMotion, or a 120Hz refresh rate of any kind. Instead, it’s still locked to 60Hz. This is an incredibly frustrating decision that I can’t quite wrap my head around.

Apple touts the iPad mini’s OLED screen as offering significantly faster pixel response time than the previous generation’s LCD panel, leading to improvements like smoother scrolling and reduced motion blur.

I’ve noticed that things like swiping between Home Screen pages, scrolling social media, and system animations are noticeably smoother. They aren’t, however, as smooth as an Apple device with a ProMotion display, and they’re not a substitute for a higher refresh-rate display.

I’m sure Apple knows the iPad mini’s market, and it seems to have decided not to prioritize ProMotion based on that information. However, as someone who has longed for a so-called “iPad mini Pro” for years, I’m disappointed by the decision. The new iPad mini’s screen is so much better … I just wish Apple had gone that extra step and added ProMotion. We’ve reached a point where ProMotion should be table stakes, especially after Apple brought it to the base iPhone 17 last year.

For an extra $100, you can upgrade the new iPad mini to have a nano-texture display (on the 256GB and 512GB models).

I’m a huge fan of Apple’s nano-texture display and have it on my 14-inch MacBook Pro. On the iPad mini, I think it makes even more sense.

The iPad mini is ultra-portable, and you naturally carry it around and use it in different lighting environments. The nano-texture glass helps reduce reflections and glare in a wide variety of lighting conditions. I also really like the combination of the iPad mini’s book-like size and the nano-texture finish.

There is a slight tradeoff in color vibrancy compared to a glossy OLED screen, as on other Apple devices with nano-texture, but it’s a very minor difference in my experience. The screen still looks fantastic.

One of the more interesting changes with the new iPad mini is something Apple calls the “Acoustic Display.” Instead of traditional speakers with visible grilles, Apple has developed a new system that uses the display itself to produce sound.

Essentially, Apple has designed special woofers that vibrate the display to produce low and midrange frequencies. For higher frequencies, custom tweeters are hidden between the glass and aluminum enclosure. Apple says this new system delivers louder audio, “punchier” bass, and clearer highs, despite the iPad mini’s significantly thinner design.

In practice, I think the new iPad mini sounds great. I’d choose headphones or an external speaker for serious music or video consumption, but day-to-day the iPad mini’s built-in speakers are perfectly adequate. (I’d bet that this Acoustic Display technology shows up in future iPhones too, and the iPad mini is serving as a test bed of sorts.)

The Acoustic Display also plays an important role in another major upgrade: water and dust resistance. The new iPad mini is IP67 rated, which means it can be immersed in 1 meter of freshwater for up to 30 minutes. It’s the first iPad to have an official water-resistance rating.

Adding water resistance to the iPad mini is particularly notable given its size and portability. I naturally find myself wanting to take it everywhere, and water resistance makes that more feasible.

One use case where all these improvements really come together is reading. The thinner and lighter design, nano-texture glass, and water resistance make the new iPad mini the most compelling iPad yet to serve as an e-reader.

The new iPad mini is powered by Apple’s A20 Pro chip, which I already covered in detail in my iPhone 18 Pro review. The short version: the A20 Pro chip gives you plenty of power for anything you can throw at the iPad mini today.

One detail worth calling out is that Apple uses two different versions of the A20 Pro in the iPad mini. The 128GB and 256GB models feature a five-core CPU and 16-core Neural Engine, while the 512GB model gets a six-core CPU and Dual 16-core Neural Engine. All three configurations feature the same seven-core GPU.

I don’t think anyone should buy the 512GB version of the iPad mini just for those extra cores. You should pick your iPad mini configuration based on how much storage you need, not the version of the A20 Pro chip. You don’t need to worry about performance with the new iPad mini. And perhaps most importantly, the A20 Pro chip ensures the iPad mini has enough headroom for the future.

There’s been a lot of consternation about where the iPad mini fits in a world where the iPhone Duo also now exists. It’s a fair question. After all, when the iPhone Duo is unfolded, the two devices share a similar form factor … but that’s really where the similarities end.

The iPad mini offers the full-fledged, unapologetic iPadOS experience. It supports the full multitasking prowess of an iPad Pro, including windowing and the menu bar. The new iPad mini also supports extended display mode, so you can plug it into an external display and extend your iPad experience there.

The iPad mini also gets iPadOS app layouts, and most importantly, a desktop-class browsing experience in Safari. It’s a remarkably capable device in a remarkably compact form factor. It fits where other iPads can’t, yet it runs the same version of iPadOS as other iPads.

The new iPad mini does all of that, but better than before. The thinner, lighter design paired with smaller bezels gives the new iPad mini a meaningful visual refresh. The added water resistance means you can do even more with the compact and pocketable iPad mini design.

But all of this comes at a higher price of $699. This marks the second price increase for the iPad mini this year. It started the year at $499, rose to $599 as part of Apple’s broader price increases in June, and is now $699 as of this refresh.

The new iPad mini also still starts with 128GB of storage. Increasing the base storage to 256GB would’ve helped ease some of the pain of that price increase. It’s also getting increasingly hard to manage a device with 128GB, particularly with the storage needs of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. The lack of ProMotion and Face ID also make the price increase sting more.

Ultimately, the iPad mini form factor is a joy to use. The design feels great in the hand, and having the full iPadOS experience in such a compact device remains impressive. It’s not quite the “iPad mini Pro” I’ve always wanted, but it’s big upgrade to a form factor that I’ve always loved.

#3288. I played the Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2, and it’s even better than my childhood memories

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a joy to revisit from start to finish thanks to its gorgeous 4K visuals, full orchestral score, and slick modern controls. It may not be a brand-new adventure, but it’s the definitive remake fans have always wanted and easily the best way to experience the legendary game that started it all.

Smart quality-of-life upgrades throughout

Intuitive, modern controls with gyro support

Orchestral soundtrack feels grand and cinematic

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Platforms: Nintendo Switch 2Price: $69.99 / $59.99 (digital), £58.99 / £49.99 (digital), $109.95 AUD / $94.95 AUD (digital)Release Date: November 4, 2026Genre: Action-adventure

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is exactly what I wanted from one of the most anticipated remakes yet. Instead of a reimagining, it’s a one-to-one remake that does exactly what it needs to — overhauling the N64 classic’s visuals and gameplay — but despite being based on a 28-year-old game, it still manages to feel fresh.

Even though the updated art style initially drew criticism, it really grew on me over the course of my 20+ hour playthrough. From the details in the fabric of Link’s clothes to the way the water moved around him while diving for rupees, the game’s overhauled graphics continued to impress me. In fact, I had to remind myself to cut through the grass and shrubbery in Hyrule Field to look for items instead of just staring at it in awe. Then to top it all off, the new orchestral score makes the game feel incredibly cinematic.

Although Nintendo didn’t reimagine Ocarina of Time, it did take common complaints to heart. Being able to jump on command is big enough on its own, but the game makes exploring dungeons easier too with a fully controllable camera and having key gear mapped to your D-pad instead of hidden away behind menus. Gyro aiming also makes solving puzzles with your bow or grabbing Gold Skulltulas with your hookshot feel that much more rewarding.

Is it worth experiencing the boy without a fairy transform into the Hero of Time once again on the Nintendo Switch 2 though? Find out in my full review.

When it comes to classics like Ocarina of Time, it’s hard not to remember how you experienced them with rose-tinted glasses. Just go back and play the original on Nintendo Switch Online to see what I mean. With the new remake on the Nintendo Switch 2 though, it looks and feels the way my childhood imagination always convinced me it did.

The Great Deku Tree looks absolutely massive — and equally imposing — when you’re standing in front of it as Young Link in the game’s intro. The same is true when you leave Kokiri Forest for the first time and step out into the rolling expanse of Hyrule Field, greeted by the owl Kaepora Gaebora. The world of Ocarina of Time is nowhere near as big as that of Breath of the Wild or Tears of the Kingdom, but the remake’s visuals certainly fooled me into thinking it was, despite replaying the game multiple times over the years.

The locations and dungeons you visit throughout the game are quite impressive too, especially given how much work Nintendo put into the small details. From dust hanging in the air as the sun pours into the Temple of Time to seeing individual strands of hay in the scarecrow Pierre, my eyes couldn’t stop going over the little things as I played through Ocarina of Time on the Switch 2 in docked mode on my TV.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The visuals alone make this remake easy to recommend, but it’s the modern controls that truly made me feel like the Hero of Time.

Navigating a 3D world with a single analog stick was a real pain, which is why Nintendo implemented modern camera controls in the Ocarina of Time remake. They work just as you’d expect them to, with your controller’s right analog stick giving you 360 degrees of freedom to look around and explore Hyrule as you see fit.

Personally, I found these new camera controls to be tremendously useful when solving puzzles in dungeons and especially as I hunted for Gold Skulltulas. Switching to Z-targeting when taking on large groups of enemies was a quick reminder of just how far we’ve come with this remake.

The biggest upgrade when it comes to controlling Link though is the addition of a dedicated jump button. Timing my jumps and making it safely onto narrow platforms was a whole lot easier this time around. Likewise, I found the new gyro aiming to feel just as natural when using my bow and arrow or even when casting my line while fishing.

Ocarina of Time’s menus have been given the same attention to detail and visual overhaul as the rest of the game. The main menu is much more polished, but instead of having to jump back into it over and over again to change your equipment, you can do so using a new Breath of the Wild-style pop-up overlay. With a tap of either bumper, you can browse through and equip whatever you need for a particular puzzle or enemy on the fly, which really helps speed up both combat and traversal.

While you use this menu to switch from your slingshot to your boomerang, donning a new mask or, more importantly, switching boots is even easier. Just like in Ocarina of Time’s 3DS remake, your boots are now mapped to down on the D-pad. Nintendo did streamline some aspects of the game’s dungeons, but this small tweak alone makes the dreaded Water Temple a whole lot easier to traverse.

As for Link’s fairy companion Navi, she’s still right by your side throughout your journey. However, there are far fewer interruptions, and when she does speak, you actually want to listen. A big part of this comes down to the fact that Navi is now fully voice-acted and doesn’t constantly nag you with “Hey!”, “Listen!”, or “Watch out!”.

Whether it’s Zelda’s Lullaby or the Sun’s Song, music plays a pivotal role in Ocarina of Time from start to finish. From your namesake instrument down to the various themes that greet you when you enter Goron City or the Lost Woods, this remake was quite literally music to my ears.

For starters, the entire soundtrack was re-recorded with a full live orchestra. Ocarina of Time has never sounded this good. Alongside punchier battle sound effects, every track sounded superb in surround sound through my TV setup, and held up just as well using virtual surround in handheld mode.

Nintendo also took the Switch 2’s built-in microphone into account. If you know Epona’s Song or another tune by heart, you don't even have to input the notes using A, B, X, Y, and the bumpers — you can simply hum the melody and the game will do the rest. There’s also an optional electronic ocarina accessory from Hori that pairs with the game if you want to physically play the notes yourself, though I didn’t have a chance to test it out firsthand.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time may not be a brand-new adventure in the Zelda universe, but it’s by far the best way to replay this timeless classic. Its stunning 4K visuals keep your eyes glued to the screen, while the completely redone orchestral soundtrack will linger in your head long after you put down the controller. Meanwhile, the addition of modern controls alongside small but significant quality-of-life upgrades make what used to feel tedious feel completely natural.

If you played and loved the original, this remake is an absolute must. If Breath of the Wild was your first taste of the series, Ocarina of Time lets you experience the foundational game that made modern 3D Zelda possible, complete with all the polish you’d expect from Nintendo. There has never been a better time to strap on your sword and shield, step out of Kokiri Forest, and see what you’ve been missing.

#3287. Why are premium domains so expensive?

A normal .com costs about $11 a year to register. The best names can sell for millions. Here is why.

Premium domains are expensive because each name exists only once, and short, memorable ones are long gone. Registries and owners price them on demand. They help brands get remembered, but they do not boost Google rankings, and some renew at premium prices.

Registering a normal .com address is cheap. Since 1 November, registrars pay Verisign, which runs .com, $10.97 a year per name, after a 7% rise, Domain Name Wire reported. Yet Voice.com sold for $30M in 2019.

The gap comes down to scarcity. Every domain name exists only once, and the short, clear words people remember were registered decades ago. No amount of money creates a second one.

Some premium names have never been registered. Registries, the companies that run each extension, flag short or keyword-rich names in advance and charge more for them. Some keep charging a premium every year.

Most famous premium names, though, are resold by people or companies that already own them. The owner sets the price, which is usually negotiable. After the sale, these names normally renew at the standard rate.

A short, familiar name is easier to say, type and remember, so more people find a business without searching for it. It can also make a young company look established. Swedish startup Lovable recently took over lovable.com from an Italian lingerie brand.

What a premium name does not buy is a better Google ranking. “Keywords in a TLD do not give any advantage or disadvantage in search,” Google says.

Demand can lift a whole extension: the AI boom pushed .ai, Anguilla’s country code, past 1M registrations. It earned the island $80M from January to July, nearly half its government revenue, the Jamaica Gleaner reported. Slovenia’s .si saw 20,000 sign-ups in a day after Trump renamed AI “Super Intelligence”.

The sticker price can mislead. A domain sold for $1 in its first year may renew at $20, and some registry premiums stay expensive every year. Before buying, check the first-year price, the renewal fee and what you would pay to transfer it.

#3286. Apple explains the $400 premium for the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display

Apple argued that the touchscreen isn’t the headline feature of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, merely a bonus.

The headline should instead be the quality of the display itself – with the company effectively suggesting that the $400 premium is positively cheap for what you’re getting …

Apple published a white paper in which it argues that the latest MacBook Pro display is essentially a smaller version of its professional reference monitor, the Studio Display XDR.

$400 for the screen and new design isn’t my issue, my issue is the cost of storage and memory. $600 more to go from 24gb to 48gb or nearly a grand for 64gb. You can easily spend nearly double the cost of the machine just getting it to a semi-future proof spec.

Given that this costs anywhere from $2,899 to $3,599 just for a display (albeit a significantly larger one with a correspondingly higher resolution), this does put into perspective that $400 extra over the MacBook Pro with the standard screen. Here’s what Apple has to say about it:

PROLED XDR display, the best display in a pro laptop, finally overcomes these historic limitations. For the first time, a MacBook Pro display uses tandem OLED technology, delivering up to 1000 nits of sustained full-screen brightness, 2000 nits of peak high dynamic range (HDR) and standard dynamic range (SDR) brightness, and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio with accurate, per-pixel black levels.

It’s driven in real time by an all-new display engine in M5 Pro and M5 Max, which continuously compensates each pixel for content, usage, temperature, and ambient conditions—delivering creative precision out of the box and protecting panel lifespan over time. And a unique manufacturing process ensures panel-to-panel consistency and minimizes off-axis color shift, a first for any OLED laptop.

As Macworld spotted, that’s almost identical to the company’s description of the the Studio Display XDR.

In fact, the PROLED XDR in the MacBook Pro is the only display other than the Studio Display XDR that supports Apple CMF 2026, the next generation of CIE 1931. Apple says CMF 2026 “more precisely aligns the appearance of the display with an ideal D65 illuminant—the standard reference for white—and significantly improves appearance matching across display technologies, which is important for workflows that use multiple displays side by side.”

Resolution aside, the other specs are identical with just one exception: the contrast ratio. As for that exception, the MacBook display comes out on top with a 10 million to 1 contrast ratio, in contrast with the Studio Display XDR’s one million.

Does this change your own perspective of the price premium of the OLED model? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

#3285. T-Mobile launches 5-gigabit fiber for $90/mo with 10-year price guarantee

T-Mobile has announced a new 5 gigabit fiber broadband service priced at $90 a month, starting today. The company also says that if you sign up now, the price is guaranteed not to increase for a full decade …

The company now offers a total of 4 different home broadband plans with fiber connections:

All pricing is based on choosing autopay billing and without taxes and fees. The company says that for a limited time you can also get bill credits equivalent to two months free, and $300 in virtual prepaid cards provided you don’t cancel within the first year.

The company says its fastest ever service is intended for the most demanding households.

With 5 Gig, busy households have the bandwidth for more people and devices to be online at the same time — whether that’s gaming, working or keeping a growing number of smart home devices connected. And because T‑Mobile Fiber runs on a 100% fiber-optic connection directly to the home, customers get fast, consistent performance with symmetrical speeds, meaning uploads are just as fast as downloads. That matters because households aren’t just downloading. Video calls, security cameras, cloud backups and more depend on fast upload speeds, too […]

“Between online gaming, smart devices and AI-powered tools, there’s more happening online in our households than ever,” said chief commercial officer Andre Almeida. “Our fastest 5 Gig plan gives customers incredible capacity for everything they’re doing today, with room to grow for whatever comes next.”

As always, you have to check the small print on price guarantees, which in this case is as follows:

Taxes & fees, voluntary equipment or speed upgrades, select limited-time promotions, per-use charges, third-party services, and network management practices aren’t included.

The most obvious potential gotcha is that broadband speeds will continue to increase over the years, and choosing to upgrade to a faster service at a later date eliminates the price guarantee.

You can check availability on the company’s website.

#3284. Aformic raises $6.95M to move its factory robots into AI data centres

The South Carolina startup's self-driving forklifts and carts already move parts for Toyota, 3M and Oshkosh Defense.

Aformic, which makes self-driving forklifts and carts for factories, raised a $6.95M seed round led by Veteran Ventures Capital. It says it has more than $34M in orders and plans new robots for building and maintaining AI data centres.

Industrial robotics startup Aformic has raised a $6.95M seed round led by Veteran Ventures Capital, the company said on Wednesday. ff Venture Capital, Mana Ventures, Red Beard Ventures and Alamo Angels also took part.

Based in Duncan, South Carolina, Aformic makes self-driving forklifts and carts that move parts and materials around factories and warehouses. They navigate without tape or markers on the floor, and its Qursor software plans their routes and assigns tasks.

The company was spun out of AIUT, a Polish industrial automation group, and still has an engineering and production centre in Gliwice, Poland.

Aformic says it has won more than $34M in orders and has hundreds of robots in use. Its customers include Toyota, Hitachi, 3M, Hyundai Mobis and Oshkosh Defense. Over the past year, it says, its robots drove more than 186,000 miles inside customers’ plants.

“AFORMIC was built to automate the industries that matter,” said chief executive Michal Fiuk, a US Army veteran.

The money will fund more engineers and sales staff, work on Qursor, and new robots for other jobs, including helping to build and maintain AI data centres. Data centre builders say a shortage of skilled workers is now one of their biggest bottlenecks.

Investors are backing factory robots in a big way. Earlier this week, Tutor Intelligence raised $75M from a16z for robots that customers rent by the hour, and Toyota spin-out Walden Robotics launched with $300M in July.

Adobe Premiere mobile users will soon be able to add licensed music from two of the world’s biggest music companies to their videos. Here are the details.

Adobe today announced a partnership with Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group that will let Premiere mobile users browse and add music from popular artists to their videos directly within the app.

By combining music from two of the world’s leading music companies with Premiere mobile’s pro-level video editing tools, we’re making it easier for you to discover the tracks you love, shape your video around the music and share your stories, all in one free app

As Adobe explains, the tracks will be licensed for personal, non-commercial use. The company added that Adobe Stock Audio will remain available for projects that require commercially licensed music.

Here’s what users will be able to do once the new features become available, per Adobe:

The new music library will complement Premiere mobile’s existing features, which include tools for cleaning up audio recordings, advanced video editing capabilities, and AI-powered asset generation through Adobe Firefly.

The company didn’t provide an exact date for when the new music library will become available, nor whether tracks from both companies will arrive at the same time. The announcement also didn’t specify how many songs will be included or whether the agreements cover the companies’ entire music catalogs. Adobe said only that the new features are “coming soon.”
