#3269. This Hidden Device Could Free Up Gigawatts of Grid Power

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Variable frequency drives can slash motors’ power use

Zurich-based ABB is one of several manufacturers of variable frequency drives (VFDs), such as this ACH580. VFDs could help make the millions of electric motors running in industrial facilities more energy efficient.

This article was originally published by Canary Media.

America’s energy supply crunch is driving a surge of federal and private investment in new electricity generation—from polluting gas turbines to cleaner developments like solar farms and geothermal plants. But gigawatts of power are already available for the taking across the U.S. economy in the form of wasted energy from an unexpected source: motors.

Some 50 million electric motors drive the fans, pumps, and compressors found in virtually every factory and building. Together, they gobble enough electricity to equal nearly a third of total U.S. power demand. Often, the motors use far more energy than they actually need to keep America’s machines humming.

Companies can install devices known as variable frequency drives, or VFDs, to make motors run super efficiently. Yet adoption remains relatively low, in part because of the perceived hassle of retrofitting equipment and because they’re typically not required. On average, only 16 percent of motor systems at industrial facilities and 4 percent of commercial-sector motors use VFDs, according to a 2021 market report by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

However, there are now more reasons than ever to equip the nation’s motors with power-saving devices, energy experts and device manufacturers say. They’re urging federal agencies, utilities, and deep-pocketed tech giants to spur a wider rollout of VFDs through financial incentives and efficiency standards.

For one, slashing motors’ power use would free up grid capacity for large electricity users like data centers and electric vehicles, they argue. It would help curb costs for factories that are switching from fossil-fueled heating systems to electrified, motor-based solutions like heat pumps—all at a time when industrial power prices are climbing fast. Plus, VFD technology has become far more sophisticated and less expensive to install than earlier iterations.

“This is low-hanging fruit that gives a lot [of energy] back and is reasonably simple,” Nik Sawe, a senior policy analyst at the nonpartisan think tank Energy Innovation, says of the technology.

Energy-wise, the main problem with electric motors is that they’re always running at full capacity. Consider an office building, which empties out in the evening. The heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning system can wind down in those hours, with dampers and valves restricting the flow of cold or hot air. But the motors and fans that drive the whole setup are still working in the background, wasting energy.

VFD technology, such as the Danfoss iC7 series, has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings trying to combat rising electricity costs. Danfoss Drives

VFDs are electronic controllers with temperature sensors that continually adjust the speed of motors, automatically ramping up or down to match demand. The technology, which is also called adjustable speed drives, has the potential to curb a motor’s energy use by around 40 to 60 percent, says Neal Elliott, director emeritus of the American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy.

All those energy reductions add up. Toyota, for example, installed VFDs on over 200 motors inside the HVAC system at its auto manufacturing plant in Georgetown, Kentucky, as part of a US $1.25 million pilot project in 2015. The automaker saved more than $700,000 in annual electricity costs thanks to the VFDs, and it continues to use the technology at other manufacturing facilities across the U.S., the company said by email.

“We’ve known for many, many years that there’s a huge opportunity for energy savings by varying the speed of the motor,” says Elliott, who noted that he literally wrote the book on energy-efficient motor systems in 2002.

Certain aspects of the technology have historically held the drives back since they debuted in the late 1960s. Measuring the flow of water, air, refrigerant—whatever is moving through the system that the motors are driving—was for decades an expensive engineering process. Accurately controlling motors to deliver the right amount of juice, at just the right time, faced similar issues.

But recent advances in sensors and machine-learning algorithms have significantly slashed the cost and complexity of using drives, Elliott says. Modern VFDs have also benefited from the increased production of advanced power chips that are used in high-voltage applications such as electric vehicles and solar power inverters.

Another long-standing challenge has been that commercial and industrial building developers often prioritize reducing upfront costs over netting long-term energy savings, and so they don’t always build to the highest efficiency levels, says Zack Valdez, senior director of regulatory and industry affairs at the National Electrical Manufacturers Association, whose members include drive and motor makers.

“If the facility that you’re putting it into doesn’t require it, then oftentimes people will overlook [VFDs], because they’re just trying to build to a minimum set of energy requirements,” he says. And if companies don’t install drives from the start, they’re likely less inclined to take time to retrofit an operating system.

The trade association recently launched a pilot program with manufacturers, utilities, and energy-efficiency groups to collect real-world data about how VFDs reduce motors’ electricity use and lower utility bills. The goal is to demonstrate how the technology can benefit not only individual facilities but also the wider grid—giving utilities a concrete reason to provide rebates for industrial customers.

Proponents say they hope the results will help the U.S. Department of Energy shape future efficiency measures and incentives that encourage adoption of the drives, including in federally owned buildings. Despite the Trump administration’s open hostility toward home appliance and equipment mandates, agency staff have apparently been receptive to discussing solutions that could meet the soaring power needs of data centers.

“If you added a drive to all the motors that are out there, you could provide [power for] up to five years of data center growth without having to build any new generation,” says Kirk Anderson, director of government relations and public affairs for ABB. The global manufacturing giant makes VFDs domestically near Milwaukee.

Anderson floated the idea of having tech companies help pay for factory owners to install VFDs to free up room on the grid. After all, hyperscalers are already spending many billions of dollars to revive shuttered nuclear plants, support next-generation geothermal projects, deploy fleets of grid-scale batteries, and supercharge the build-out of gas turbines and power plants.

“Instead of ‘bring your own power,’ it should be ‘offset your own power,’” he says, referring to a growing effort by states to get data centers to secure their own power resources and prevent rising costs for regular customers.

Michael Reckamp, the director of enterprise strategy for Danfoss Drives, North America, another VFD manufacturer, said that despite the traditionally low adoption rates, the technology has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings as rising electricity costs and other grid-wide challenges make it harder to justify wasting energy.

Still, “it hasn’t permeated enough to get everyone utilizing it,” he says. “In the current situation, where we’re having so many issues with grids, brownouts, and now data centers wanting to take the load, I think there should be a renewed focus on putting drives out there to really reduce the stress on the grid and improve energy savings.”

Maria Gallucci is a clean-energy reporter with Canary Media.

#3266. Google will spend $15B on data centres in Malaysia over two years

New campuses in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan add to Malaysia's place as Southeast Asia's data centre hub.

Google plans to spend $15B in Malaysia in 2027 and 2028 on data centres, cloud operations, water, power and training. It will expand its Selangor campus and build new ones in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan, where it is also funding a $160M water plant.

Google plans to spend $15B on data centres and cloud operations in Malaysia in 2027 and 2028, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday. The money will also go into local water supplies, power generation and training, the company said.

Google will expand its existing campus at Elmina Business Park in Selangor and build new ones in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan, Malay Mail reported. The Elmina site came from a $2B investment Google announced in May 2024.

Alphabet chief investment officer Ruth Porat announced the plan at an event in Kuala Lumpur attended by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.

“Our nation possesses the stability, the talent, the ambition to be a premier digital powerhouse in Southeast Asia,” Anwar said.

Google says building the campuses will support more than 37,000 local jobs a year and add about $1.1B a year to Malaysia’s economy. Once they are running, it expects them to sustain more than 9,000 jobs.

Water is a big part of the deal. Earlier this week, Google said it would fund a $160M reservoir and treatment plant in Negeri Sembilan. It will supply 65 million litres of drinking water a day to the data centre and nearby communities.

Water has become a flashpoint for Google elsewhere. Its $15B India data centre has faced protests over local supplies, and on Indonesia’s Batam island, near Singapore, residents have protested dry taps as data centres spread.

Malaysia has become Southeast Asia’s main data centre hub, thanks to low costs, reliable infrastructure and its closeness to Singapore. Oracle, Amazon, Alibaba and ByteDance are all expanding there. The country has more than 6 GW of planned capacity, the largest pipeline in the region.

More money may follow. In late October, Anwar said SoftBank’s Masayoshi Son plans about $50B of AI investment in Malaysia, though SoftBank has not confirmed the figure.

The deal mirrors one Google made in Europe. In September, it said it would put €13B into Finland over the same two years.

#3265. Sam Altman just renamed himself ‘Ram Altman’ in U.S. Midterms aftermath — the panic is setting in, but is the AI bubble starting to crack?

Sam's memory loss may be one for the record books

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For the last year, covering PC hardware has felt like reporting from the apocalypse. We’ve all been living through “RAMageddon,” watching RAM prices rise by hundreds of dollars, and listening to industry CEOs warn us that supply chain relief wouldn’t arrive until 2028.

But overnight, the tech landscape has started to violently shift. Look no further than OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

The guy who recently went on a podcast to tell you that local PC memory is a “terrible” allocation of scarce resources just executed a head-spinning PR pivot — playfully renaming his X account to “Ram Altman” and saying he's argued for local consumer memory "for a long time."

So why the sudden switch up? Well, you saw things start to play out over the past week. Financial markets have begun pushing back against the endless cash-pit of cloud AI data centers (with one exception: AMD, but we’ll get to that).

And now, the 2026 midterm results have introduced a massive new variable that may fundamentally alter the supply chain. Bloomberg reported that key wins will put 50% of proposed data centers under more scrutiny and pushback.

If this holds, the hyperscaler data center boom just hit a regulatory brick wall — and everyday PC builders are going to be the winners soon.

To understand why your next GPU or DDR5 memory kit may get cheaper, you have to look at what Democrat majorities in Congress mean for Big Tech’s infrastructure obsession.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Hyperscalers like Microsoft, Amazon and OpenAI have grand plans to blanket the country with gigawatt-guzzling AI data centers (or as OpenAI just soft-rebranded them to, “Compute Campuses”). But the incoming legislative majorities carry strict, vocal mandates on environmental protections, EPA oversight and energy grid conservation.

The era of tech giants getting fast-tracked, rubber-stamped permits to drain local power grids for their LLM training is over.

The era of tech giants getting fast-tracked, rubber-stamped permits to drain local power grids for their LLM training is over. If OpenAI and Microsoft cannot physically secure the permits and power to build their server farms, they can’t (or won't) buy the silicon. If they can’t buy the silicon, the massive vacuum of enterprise demand that has been starving the consumer market shrinks.

Foundries will have no choice but to pivot their advanced manufacturing wafers back to standard consumer GPUs and DDR5 memory to keep their revenues flowing.

When you look at the midterm results, Altman’s sudden rebranding makes sense. I don’t have a direct line to him to figure out his emotional state. But if I were in his shoes, I’d see this bottleneck coming and quietly panic.

When called out on his podcast comments, Altman went on the defensive: “I actually do want the world to have tons of memory and people to put as much as they want in their computer… I have been arguing for the world to ramp up memory production for a long time.”

People should always be in control of the future. OpenAI is against the notion that it would be acceptable for people to be relegated to a role of doing things that “AI systems think makes sense to reward in humans”. People should not cede control of the future to superintelligence, and that requirement should ultimately constrain AI progress.November 4, 2026

Let the BS detector run on that for a second… It is incredibly convenient to suddenly champion local memory rights, just as your cloud expansion plans potentially hit a political (and environmental) roadblock.

The fear is real — the blank-check era of unregulated data center expansion is surely dying. And if the cloud is capped, OpenAI has to figure out how to run its models locally on your hardware.

I would love nothing more than to post unadulterated hopecore and declare an end to RAMageddon right here and now. But to be a trusted voice, you have to turn the BS detector on yourself sometimes. And this week, AMD just changed the conversation.

If the data center bubble is truly bursting, someone forgot to tell CEO Lisa Su. AMD reported a 45% year-over-year surge in revenue for Q3, and KeyBanc reiterated an “overweight” rating on its stock. In Wall Street speak, an overweight rating is an aggressive “BUY” signal, meaning analysts expect the company to outperform the rest of the market.

And the reason is exactly what you assume: massive 97% data center growth. They aren’t scaling back; they’re selling every single EPYC processor and Instinct GPU they can possibly print, actively fighting to secure more foundry capacity.

If hyperscalers are still handing AMD blank checks for enterprise silicon, the foundries have zero incentive to pivot back to the budget consumer hardware we desperately need.

We are officially standing in the middle of a massive tech standoff.

On one side, you have AMD’s earnings proving that the tech giants still have bottomless wallets and an insatiable appetite for silicon. On the other side, you have the Midterm shift of power that may see Washington cut off the physical power grids and data center built out needed for that silicon.

We aren’t completely out of the woods, and AMD’s financial juggernaut proves that 2027 is still going to be a rough year for PC builders. But the hardware hoarders are finally losing their unregulated grip on the supply chain.

Washington may step in, and “Ram Altman” knows it. If you can hold the line on upgrading your rig just a little longer, the incoming red tape might just trigger the local compute renaissance we’ve been waiting for.

Smart city deployments have historically relied on cameras, sensors, and dashboards that capture data without delivering timely insight. This guide traces the progression from automation and perception to prediction, agentic coordination, and physical AI, where urban systems continuously perceive conditions, reason about them, and act within a tiered edge architecture spanning far-edge sensors, regional infrastructure, and the cloud. Royalty income carried the quarter as margins and cash conversion stayed strong.

Management reported that the company completed its first full quarter as a public entity following its May initial public offering and expanded its Midland Basin footprint through a new 35,000-acre dedication from Double Eagle. The company remains focused on its strategy of generating high-margin royalty and fee income through surface use and water infrastructure agreements while maintaining a capital-light operating structure that requires minimal capital investment.

Now I am pleased to turn the call over to Gregory.

Gregory Phillip Pipkin Jr.: Thanks, Chris, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Eagle Rock's third quarter 26 earnings call. We once again delivered strong results, a testament to the continued dedication of our employees, the support of our ownership group, and the collaboration of our business partners. We are grateful to have them all in our corner. Adjusted EBITDA was $34 million for the third quarter on strength in our higher margin segments. Free cash flow is approximately $32 million representing a 93% free cash flow conversion rate. This robust cash flow generation has already allowed us to repay as of October 31, approximately 25% of the debt we raised to fund the Intrepid Ranch acquisition we announced in August.

Positive momentum continued after the end of the quarter as yesterday, we announced a significant new acreage dedication from Double Eagle. Our agreement with Double Eagle V dedicates 35 thousand acres in Midland and Glasscock Counties to us increasing their total acreage dedicated to Eagle Rock by 50% to over 100 thousand acres. Importantly, this acreage dedication underscores the strength of our capital light business model generating additional royalty revenue without requiring any capital investment by Rock. The Double Eagle V dedication is yet another example of how our footprint assets, and capabilities combined with our relationship with Double Eagle creates meaningful value for our shareholders.

In addition to the Double Eagle V dedication, we bolstered our acreage footprint through 2 bolt on acquisitions that added approximately 2,000 acres in the Midland Basin for less than 10x EBITDA. These ranches directly offset our existing footprint in Glasscock and Reagan Counties and further strengthen our ability to commercialize our surface acreage across the Midland Basin. Although I refer to these transactions as bolt ons, I cannot underscore enough how excited we are about what these acquisitions combined with our new acreage dedication mean for Eagle Rock. These transactions enhance our dedicated acreage and tie our own organic acquisition strategy directly into our larger shareholders development footprint.

They also expand our water resource and storage capabilities, adding approximately 50 thousand barrels per day of brackish water supply capacity 2 million barrels of above ground storage, and increased our produced water disposal capacity which supports monetization of the entire Double Eagle dedicated footprint. Taken together, these transactions reflect continued integration and densification of our position across the Midland Basin. Our acquisition pipeline remains robust and continues to grow and we see a range of additional opportunities across the portfolio. Generally in the 500- to 15 thousand-acre range, that we believe fit our strategy. Our approach to every acquisition remains the same.

We access the development potential of the asset, and the strategic fit within our portfolio, and we evaluate whether it is accretive and creates shareholder value. We view these recent transactions along with the Intrepid Ranch acquisition as a demonstration of our ability to move quickly and decisively when a deal fits our portfolio and our strategy. As a reminder, Eagle Rock owns or controls approximately 288 thousand surface acres across the Delaware and Midland sub basins of the Permian. 100% of our revenues are derived from royalties and fees, generated from surface land use that requires minimal capital exposure.

Our surface use agreements cover a broad range of activities on our land, and as operators' needs evolve in a fast changing environment, we are able to mutually agree to terms that benefit both parties. This setup creates a continuous and growing set of opportunities to capture additional value over time. We serve more than 90 different customers, including many well capitalized leading E&Ps. Double Eagle, 1 of the most active private operators in the Midland Basin, is our largest shareholder and a key strategic relationship for us. And we also benefit from equally deep relationships elsewhere across the basin.

Eagle Rock is built for growth, Our base business is already expanding, and acquisitions provide another meaningful avenue to scale our platform. Our management teams and owners deep industry relationships and regional expertise, give us a distinct advantage in identifying and executing acquisitions that complement our existing footprint and build on our high growth core. Third quarter's results reflect that foundation at work, so let me elaborate on the quarter's highlights. Surface use royalties and surface use revenue both became a larger share of our revenue mix in the third quarter. Because they carry no associated cost of sales, that shift supported our strong margin performance.

#3261. Apple announces Fitness+ Gym Strength program with personalized workout plans

Apple wants to help you get stronger. Apple Fitness+ is expanding to the gym with a new strength training experience. Gym Strength is now available in beta, bringing personalized workout plans, exercise demonstrations, and Apple Watch logging to your lifting routine.

Gym Strength creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment. After you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weight you logged.

The feature is designed for a range of experience levels, from people trying strength training for the first time to experienced lifters looking to make progress. It also aims to help anyone who wants to build a more consistent routine.

When building a plan, you choose your workout days and the body areas you want to focus on. You can select five exercises per workout, which Apple estimates will take about 20–30 minutes, or seven exercises for about 45–60 minutes, depending on your pace.

Each workout recommends exercises, reps, sets, and how much weight to lift.

You move through the workout at your own pace, with short video demonstrations from Apple Fitness+ trainers available for each exercise. The demonstrations can be expanded to show the movement from three different angles.

Apple says Gym Strength includes over 350 exercises across more than 30 types of strength training equipment, including dumbbells, kettlebells, suspension trainers, cable machines, and barbells. Dumbbells are the minimum equipment requirement.

Plans account for the equipment available to you, so the experience can work in a commercial gym or a home gym.

If a machine is occupied or you’re training somewhere with different equipment, you can swap equipment or choose an alternative exercise with a similar movement and body focus. You can also add sets or skip exercises.

Gym Strength requires an iPhone running iOS 27.3 or an iPad running iPadOS 27.3. An Apple Watch running watchOS 27.3 optionally lets you view exercises and log reps and weight from your wrist, while tracking heart rate and calories burned.

Gym Strength also introduces Training Note, an optional feature powered by Apple Intelligence that previews workouts, explains progression, and highlights milestones. Training Note requires an Apple Intelligence–enabled iPhone or iPad with the device set to English.

Gym Strength is included in the existing Fitness+ subscription. It joins a library of trainer-led workouts spanning 12 workout types, including Strength, HIIT, Yoga, Pilates, Core, Cycling, Rowing, Dance, Kickboxing, treadmill walking and running, and Mindful Cooldown.

Fitness+ also offers guided meditations, personalized recommendations, and Custom Plans for scheduling workouts, with new sessions added every week.

Fitness+ is also included in Apple One Premier, which costs $39.95 per month in the U.S. and bundles Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Arcade, Apple News+, and 2TB of iCloud+ storage.

I’ve been testing the iPhone 18 Pro Max ever since it launched in September, putting it through some marquee matchups against rivals like the Galaxy S26 Ultra and Pixel 11 Pro XL. Honestly, it’s the best camera phone around, thanks largely to its strong main camera performance, low-light capabilities, mechanical variable aperture, and new Pro Controls. I didn’t think another phone could come close to matching it, but I was wrong.

It’s been years since I last tested an Oppo device, mostly because stateside availability has always kept them just out of reach for the average consumer. But after putting the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max through its paces for the past month, it’s become my favorite camera phone.

You’d think its triple 200MP camera suite would be what truly puts it ahead of the pack, but it turns out to be the game-changing attachable Hasselblad lens that really seals the deal for me. Far from a gimmicky clip-on accessory, this optic unlocks the optical reach, depth, and fidelity that genuinely make it close to replacing my mirrorless camera. Here’s why.

The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is an impressive camera phones, packing a versatile 200MP triple camera setup, massive 8,000 mAh silicon-carbon battery, 6.78-inch AMOLED display, MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro processor, 80W SuperVOOC wired charging, and 50W wireless charging.

One of my colleagues already drilled down into an Oppo Find X10 Pro Max vs. iPhone 18 Pro Max photo face-off, so I’m not going to rehash why the Oppo came out on top. Instead, I’m going to show and tell you what makes the Find X10 Pro Max stand out from the many other camera phones I’ve tested this year.

First and foremost, it starts with the hardware — a triple 200MP camera system. I’ll be the first to tell you that you should never judge a camera simply by the number of megapixels it claims. You have to evaluate the rest of the equation, especially sensor sizes and apertures.

The 200MP main shooter features a large 1/1.3-inch sensor, a wide f/1.5 aperture, and OIS. Equally notable is the 200MP periscope telephoto with 3x optical zoom, boasting a sizable 1/1.56-inch sensor and f/2.1 aperture.

That telephoto sensor is critical: through sensor cropping and Oppo’s processing algorithms, it pulls off a staggering 120x digital zoom. That easily eclipses the iPhone 18 Pro Max’s 40x ceiling, giving me triple the zoom reach of Apple's flagship. In fact, the only other phone I’ve tested this year that matches that level of reach is the Pixel 11 Pro XL.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

For me, the true test is how well a phone behaves under low light — and the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is an absolute beast. Take a look at that first shot above I captured at sunset by the beach, which handles the stark contrast in lighting exceptionally well.

With the sun dipping over the horizon, the golden glow never overpowers the scene, maintaining a rich contrast across the foreground elements. But what’s even more impressive is the sheer number of stars it resolves in the process, cleanly rendering the Pleiades star cluster right alongside the twilight sky.

The Find X10 Pro Max pulls in astonishing amounts of light without relying on overly aggressive computational brightening that turns dark night skies into a noisy mess. You can see it across the rest of the sample shots above. For the best results, I recommend switching over to its "Master" mode, which lets you fine-tune the manual exposure settings to your exact liking.

Flagships aren’t just defined by their main cameras; they also live or die by versatile telephoto systems that pull you closer to distant subjects while preserving fine detail. On its own, the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max’s native periscope camera is an absolute powerhouse. Whether I’m trying to read small text on a distant street sign or resolve faint details across a landscape, it doesn't disappoint.

I can clearly tell that computational processing kicks in at longer focal lengths, but virtually all modern flagships leverage AI upscaling to draw out fine textures. Just look at the first set of shots I captured by the waterfront, where I start with the ultrawide camera and step through all the primary focal lengths all the way to 120x.

The distant building across the inlet is practically indistinguishable in the ultrawide frame, but it sharpens into view with each successive crop — culminating in a 120x capture that brings into focus the individual bricks along the exterior wall, blades of grass in the foreground, and distinct roof shingles.

You can see its resolving power in some of the other sets of images, like pulling out intricate architectural carvings across the facade of the New York Public Library and keeping street signs fully legible from across the road.

My personal favorite is the shot of the bearded dragon I captured through its glass enclosure. What’s impressive is the staggering amount of detail, which makes it look like I had the lens parked right in front of its face based on the tight framing and definition — but in reality, I was standing about a foot away.

Lastly, I want to talk about what truly sets the Find X10 Pro Max apart: the Hasselblad telephoto converter kit. I’ve tested plenty of add-on lenses for both iPhones and Android devices over the years, and while some perform better than others, they almost always compromise on raw optical quality. What changes the game here is that this converter kit was engineered specifically to match the optics of the Find X10 Pro Max’s telephoto sensor — and the difference in output is immediately noticeable.

It's quickly become my go-to tool for nature and wildlife photography, letting me pull tight frames on distant subjects without disturbing them. The best part isn’t just the staggering amount of detail it captures — like in the first bird photo below, where you can easily make out individual feathers — it’s the authentic subject-background separation that only real optical glass can provide.

You can clearly see that depth across the sample gallery above, from the defined texture in the squirrel's bushy tail along the wooden railing to the details of nesting birds. The creamy background blur produced by this telephoto setup is remarkable, giving every frame a professional look without computational makeover. In fact, there are times when I genuinely struggle to tell the difference between these shots and those from a dedicated mirrorless camera.

After spending a full month with the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max, it’s clear that groundbreaking mobile camera innovation is thriving outside the usual suspects like Apple, Samsung, and Google. Between its versatile triple 200MP sensor array, superb low-light and astrophotography performance, and a native periscope zoom capable of reaching out to a killer 120x, it delivers every bit of the flagship-tier performance I look for.

But it’s the modular Hasselblad telephoto converter kit that truly elevates this device from a fantastic camera phone into an unmatched creative tool — delivering authentic 10x optical reach, crisp framing, and stabilized long-range shots that genuinely bridge the gap to a dedicated mirrorless setup.

#3259. Pangram’s new models spot AI fakes in images and video, it says

The AI text detection startup adds heatmaps, video uploads and browser alerts, but its accuracy figures are self-reported.

Pangram’s demo: a real photo of a restaurant whose wall mural is AI-generated (left), the Image 1.0 heatmap (centre) and the overlay (right).

Pangram launched Pangram Image 1.0 for AI images and the faster Image Flash 1.0 for video. It claims near-perfect scores on its own tests and 98.7% on the DF26 academic benchmark. Both are in its web app and API, and Image 1.0 is in its Chrome extension.

Pangram, a New York startup known for spotting AI-written text, has launched two models for detecting AI images and video, the company said on Wednesday. Pangram Image 1.0 checks still images, while the smaller, faster Pangram Image Flash 1.0 checks video frame by frame.

The image model can also draw a heatmap showing where AI content sits in a picture, such as a fake object added to a real photo. Pangram says it catches 99.2% of AI images and wrongly flags 0.27% of real ones.

In its own test, Pangram made AI copies of 100 real photos with 12 leading image generators, using prompts that closely matched each original. Image 1.0 scored 99.96% accuracy on that set. The test was designed by Pangram, not by outside reviewers.

For video, Pangram used DF26, an academic benchmark of 2,691 clips of people speaking to camera, published in September. Its authors found that both people and leading detectors did little better than chance at telling real clips from fakes.

Pangram says Flash 1.0 scores 98.7% on DF26, 29 points ahead of the next-best detector.

The new models also work on smaller images, down to 256 by 256 pixels from 512 by 512. Results below 512 pixels carry a lower-confidence warning. Pangram says it trains the models to see through compression, blur and noise, which platforms and people trying to fool detectors can add.

Image 1.0 now runs in Pangram’s Chrome extension, which flags AI content on social media, shopping and rental sites. Users can also upload videos in the web app, and the API now handles both images and video. Platforms are cracking down too: Snapchat has stopped recommending AI videos on Spotlight.

Pangram raised $9M in a round led by Menlo Ventures in July, when it first previewed image detection. Its text detector already runs on Substack.

AI detectors still make mistakes. In August, Pangram’s text tool flagged a Berkeley professor’s op-ed as partly AI-written, which she disputed.

Even Meta’s own image detector missed cropped fakes from its generator more than half the time in Reuters tests. On YouTube, a network that paid real actors to read AI scripts beat its detectors.

#3258. Bristow Group (VTOL) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Supply chain delays pressured margins even as guidance held steady.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Bristow Group Inc. (VTOL -4.13%) reported sequential revenue and earnings growth for the third quarter, supported by the integration of its recent special missions acquisition and favorable offshore energy market fundamentals. Management reaffirmed its full-year Adjusted EBITDA guidance midpoint despite persistent global supply chain challenges that have hampered aircraft modification timelines for government contracts. The company reported that its offshore energy services segment is benefiting from a multiyear contract reset cycle and a tight supply of heavy and medium helicopters globally. The company stated that it is executing a capital allocation strategy focused on fleet modernization, opportunistic share repurchases, and the maintenance of a quarterly dividend program.

Operator: Good day, everyone, and welcome to Bristow Group's third quarter of 2026 earnings call. Today's call is being recorded. After the speaker's remarks, there will be a question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question during that time, simply press star followed by the number five on your telephone keypad. At this time, I would like to turn the call over to Red Tilahun, Senior Manager of Investor Relations and Financial Reporting.

Red Tilahun: Thank you, Michael. Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Bristow Group's third quarter of 2026 earnings call. I am joined on the call today with our President and Chief Executive Officer, Chris Bradshaw, and Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, Jennifer Whalen. Before we begin, I would like to take this opportunity to remind everyone that during the course of this call, management may make forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties that are described in more detail on slide three of the investor presentation. You may access the investor presentation on our website. We will also reference certain non-GAAP financial measures such as EBITDA and free cash flow.

A reconciliation of such measures to GAAP is included in the earnings release and the investor presentation. I will now turn the call over to our President and CEO. Chris?

Chris Bradshaw: Thank you, Red. I will begin with updates on five key topics. First, safety, which remains Bristow's number one core value and highest operational priority. The company delivered on our goal of zero air accidents through the first 10 months of 2026. In occupational safety, we remain on track to achieve our third consecutive year of fewer lost workdays. I would like to thank everyone on the Bristow team for their continued focus on Target Zero, which is our commitment to zero accidents and zero harm. Second, Bristow announced strong financial results for the third quarter, and we are reaffirming the midpoint for the company's full year 2026 Adjusted EBITDA guidance, which reflects year-over-year growth of approximately 25%.

The ability to confirm this outlook, despite macro uncertainties and continued supply chain challenges, is a testament to the complementary nature of Bristow's business segments and the benefits provided by the significant geographic and customer diversity in our business model. Third, Bristow Special Missions, formerly known as Berry Aviation, has contributed strong financial results since the acquisition closed in July, and we expect this growth to accelerate in the fourth quarter and full year 2027. This acquisition has strengthened Bristow's business by adding specialized capabilities across a range of mission-critical operations and strong relationships with key military and defense customers, better positioning the company to benefit from increased defense spending trends.

Fourth, persistent industry supply chain challenges have hampered our performance. The fact that this is a familiar theme common across the aviation sector does not make it any less frustrating. Since 2020, on-time deliveries from key original equipment manufacturers have fallen by approximately 20%. Moreover, when delivery dates are missed, they have been missed by extended intervals. Slide number nine of this quarter's earning presentation summarizes extended maintenance downtime periods experienced across the helicopter industry. We have been compelled to increase inventory levels and implement other mitigations that come at a cost to the company. But unfortunately, key components continue to have increased turn times and arrive late from the suppliers.

While we are experiencing these challenges across Bristow's business, the most acute impacts can be seen in delayed aircraft modification programs for the company's new search and rescue contracts. These delays and their associated knock-on effects are depressing current margins in our government services segment. While the most readily visible effects may be contractual performance penalties, these penalties dramatically underestimate the total impact. The full knock-on effects of these delayed contract transitions include, but are not limited to, lost revenue opportunities, manpower and time spent chasing parts, cannibalization of the company's internal fleet to keep aircraft flying, and delayed aircraft lease returns, not to mention retaining additional headcount, overtime expense, and costs for outsourced third-party maintenance support.

Looking forward, based on detailed discussions and work with our key vendors, we expect these supply chain issues to stabilize during 2027, facilitating a return to historically strong margins in our government services business. Fifth and finally, Bristow's overall business is continuing to perform well despite the supply chain headwinds. Our offshore energy services business has continued to demonstrate robust profitability, and we believe positive offshore energy fundamentals and the tight supply of relevant offshore helicopters combined for more favorable industry conditions than we've seen in more than a dozen years.

I'll take some time to discuss more of the drivers poised to benefit the company later in this call, but for now, I'll hand it over to our CFO for a detailed discussion of Q3 results. Jennifer?

Jennifer Whalen: Thank you, Chris, and good morning, everyone. Before we begin, I would like to highlight that the financial results for Bristow Special Mission Inc., or BSM, from July 13th onwards are included in our consolidated financial results, following the successful closing of the acquisition in July. As a reminder, special missions, MRO, and UAS business results are included as a part of our government services segment, while the results for on-demand cargo and other remaining BSM services are reflected as a part of our other services segment.

Looking at the sequential quarter financial results on a consolidated basis, Bristow's total revenues were approximately $26 million higher in Q3 compared to Q2, while Adjusted EBITDA was approximately $10 million higher this quarter. We have tightened our guidance ranges for the remainder of the year and updated certain segments and consolidated ranges, as reflected on slide 13 of our presentation. We are also affirming our 2026 Adjusted EBITDA guidance midpoint of approximately $310 million. Turning now to our segment financial results and outlook.

Revenues in our offshore energy services, or OES segment, were $5.6 million lower in Q3, primarily due to lower utilization in Europe and higher penalties in Africa, partially offset by higher utilization and rates in the Americas. Adjusted operating income in OES was $2 million higher this quarter due to lower total operating expenses of $8.3 million and general and administrative expenses of $1.1 million, offsetting the lower revenues. The decrease in costs was primarily driven by lower utilization levels in the North Sea and lower global fuel prices.

Given the North Sea is one of our higher-cost markets in which we operate, these decreased costs, coupled with successful contract resets and growth over the past few years in key markets such as the Americas and Africa, have led to margin expansion. Our OES segment adjusted operating income margin was 27% this quarter, compared to margins in the low teens when we first began to reset our contracts towards the end of 2023. Our OES contracts are now effectively fully reset, with full-year impact of the more recent rate adjustments to be seen in 2027.

Given the continued performance of our OES business, we are tightening our 2026 guidance and increasing the adjusted operating income guidance range to $240 million-$250 million for this segment. Moving on to government services. Revenues for this segment were $17.8 million higher, primarily due to the acquisition of BSM, which contributed $16.9 million of revenues in the quarter. Revenues on the U.K. search and rescue contract were $1.6 million higher as a result of lower penalties and increased fuel revenues. Revenues on the Irish Coast Guard contract were $0.7 million lower due to higher penalties related to aircraft availability.

Adjusted operating income was $2.5 million higher, primarily due to the revenues from BSM, partially offset by higher operating expenses of $13 million and general and administrative expenses of $2.4 million, both of which were driven by the inclusion of BSM and ongoing contract transitions. While government contract transitions have continued to progress and penalties have decreased in the U.K. this quarter, overall penalties related to aircraft availability, which has been adversely impacted by continued supply chain challenges, have remained elevated throughout this year. As Chris noted, the knock-on effects of these supply chain issues have been more significant than the penalties themselves.

The net impact of these factors is included in our revised government services segment adjusted operating income range for 2026. At this time, we are updating our 2026 revenues guidance range to $470 million-$490 million and the adjusted operating income guidance range to $35 million-$45 million for this segment. As noted on our previous call, some of these transition costs will extend into early 2027, and margins on these government SAR contracts are expected to recover over time. As a reminder, these are typically 10-year base contract periods plus option years, and we still expect to generate attractive long-term cash flow yields on these important government services mandates.

2027 and beyond will also benefit from the full-year impact of the BSM acquisition and the new opportunities that are expected to arise from Bristow's new multi-mission government services offering. In our other services segment, revenues were $14 million higher this quarter, primarily due to the inclusion of BSM revenues of $9.2 million and higher activity in Australia, resulting in higher revenues of $4.8 million. Adjusted operating income for this segment was $7.4 million higher in the current quarter, mostly resulting from the increased revenues, partially offset by higher operating expenses of $4.7 million and general and administrative expenses of $1.9 million, both of which were largely related to the inclusion of BSM.

We are affirming our 2026 other services revenues and adjusted operating income guidance ranges of $155 million-$175 million and $25 million-$30 million, respectively. Lastly, the $4.5 million increase in corporate expenses this quarter is attributable to higher professional service fees related to the acquisition of BSM. Otherwise, our corporate costs remain consistent. During the quarter, we launched a new initiative aimed at retiring our legacy enterprise resource planning system and implementing a new ERP system over the course of the next year. Once live, the new ERP system is expected to save the company a meaningful amount of annual costs while offering more robust capabilities than our existing system. The new ERP is expected to go live in 2028.

We are excited to launch this project and will provide material updates as we progress. Turning now to capital allocation, cash flows, and liquidity. Our primary sources and uses of cash during the third quarter included approximately $103 million of net cash used to acquire BSM, which is subject to additional purchase price adjustments, about $29 million on shareholder returns, which include $25 million of share repurchases and nearly $4 million in cash dividends, $20.8 million of capital expenditures primarily related to progress payments on OES-configured AW189 aircraft on order, ongoing contract transitions, and normal course maintenance CapEx, principal and interest payments of $24 million, and net proceeds on an aircraft sale leaseback transaction of $19 million.

Net cash provided by operating activities increased by $20 million this quarter, while working capital showed an improvement of $17.7 million during Q3. Bristow continues to maintain a healthy cash balance and strong liquidity position. As of September 2026, our unrestricted cash balance was $233.4 million, with total available liquidity of approximately $287 million. As we continue to execute on our capital allocation program, we were pleased to return capital to shareholders this quarter through opportunistic share buybacks and additional dividend payments. The company repurchased 550,000 shares of common stock for $25 million at an average price per share of $45.64, with $96 million remaining available under the repurchase program.

Additionally, on October 29, 2026, Bristow declared a dividend of $0.125 per share of common stock, payable on November 27 to shareholders of record at the close of business on November 13. At this time, I will turn the call back to Christopher for the remarks. Chris?

Chris Bradshaw: Thank you. As noted earlier, I want to spend some time discussing industry fundamentals and the trends supporting a positive outlook for offshore energy services. Referencing slide number 14 of the earnings presentation materials, while the spot prices for crude oil and natural gas may swing up or down based upon the day's headlines, our OES customers plan their activities and expenditures based upon long-term views for commodity prices and expected financial returns. The global demand for oil and gas is expected to increase more than 12% over the next 15 years. But where will the incremental supply come from, and how secure are those barrels?

Like many industry observers, we expect offshore projects will receive an increasing share of future upstream capital investment. Deepwater projects are favorably positioned, offering attractive relative returns within the asset portfolios of oil and gas companies. Moreover, recent geopolitical events have placed an enduring emphasis on where hydrocarbon supplies are located, and the established offshore energy basins that Bristow services represent some of the most attractive and secure sources of supply. As seen on slide number 15, offshore project final investment decisions, or FIDs, are on pace to exceed $110 billion this year, following $70 billion in 2025, which would represent a year-over-year increase of more than 60%.

The outlook for next year is another 30% increase to total FIDs of approximately $144 billion in 2027. Slide 16 shows growth in the offshore rig count and utilization levels, with the utilization rate for global floating rigs expected to reach 96% next year. While the vast majority of Bristow's OES revenues, roughly 85%, support long-term production activities, an increase in the working number of offshore drilling rigs drives additional demand for helicopter services, and successful discoveries represent future production work.

Slide 17 contains additional information from Westwood Global Energy Group, which presents a comprehensive overview of the current global offshore energy infrastructure, including production facilities, drilling rigs, and offshore wind installations, as well as expectations for growth in the number of these offshore platforms over the next 10 years. As you can see, these trends point to a significant increase in demand for offshore energy logistics services, supporting a positive outlook for Bristow's business. Finally, slide 18 is an updated look at offshore helicopter capacity from Steve Robertson at Air & Sea Analytics. As you can see, effective utilization rates for the relevant models of heavy, super medium, and medium helicopters remain at or near full utilization.

This supply dynamic provides further context to the strong financial results that Jennifer reviewed earlier. In conclusion, the combination of the positive offshore energy fundamentals and the tight supply of relevant offshore helicopters represents more favorable industry conditions than we've seen in more than a dozen years. With that, let's open the line for questions. Michael?

Operator: At this time, I would like to remind everyone, in order to ask a question, please press star then number five on your telephone keypad. If you would like to withdraw your question, press star and then the number five once again. We will pause for a moment to compile the Q&A roster. The first question is from Josh Sullivan from JonesTrading. Your line is now open.

Josh Sullivan: Given the complexities on the aviation industry supply chain, obviously most of it is out of your hands, but what can you do to protect yourself from the issue while you wait for the OEMs to get their solutions in line and begin delivering on time? What can Bristow do in this time period?

Chris Bradshaw: Yes, we are taking steps to mitigate the situation as best as possible. We have increased inventory levels. We have retained additional headcount. We are spending more on overtime. We have added a second shift to the hangar that is working through the aircraft modification programs for those new search and rescue contracts. Unfortunately, all those measures come at an additional cost to the company, and you are seeing the impacts of that in Bristow's Q2 and Q3 government services financial results, thankfully being offset by strength in other parts of the business.

In addition to those measures, on the customer side, we have made some progress in getting relief on availability issues that are not under Bristow's control related to those supply chain issues you referenced. You see some benefit from that in new OES contract terms. On the government side, we have had success with our largest customer in also getting some relief on KPI penalties during this transition period, which has provided a cap on those penalties that we expect to endure at least through Q1 of 2027. That has helped some.

The main thing, though, is really working in concert with our key suppliers to help get through this aircraft modification program and to a more normalized supply chain picture stabilized in 2027. We are really focused on working through that picture with them.

Josh Sullivan: If we think about the balance of the dynamic between OEM new deliveries versus aftermarket parts, which is the bigger industry issue today?

Chris Bradshaw: Yes. By far, it is really the aftermarket and the availability of parts for existing aircraft. We have had some delays in new aircraft deliveries, as you referenced, and that is not a welcome situation clearly, but nowhere near as impactful as the overall issues with aftermarket parts availability that we need to keep the existing fleet working and operational for our customers. It is really that focus on getting parts on a more timely basis.

Josh Sullivan: I guess, kind of leads into another question. Bristow's leadership in the advanced air mobility market, upcoming flights with Electra, other partners, BETA, Elroy, et cetera. As we think about the supply chain issues with the legacy aviation industry, your diversification into the AAM market and their supply chains, is that an emerging advantage?

Chris Bradshaw: I think it could be on the margin once those aircraft are certified and operational. Thankfully, most of those aircraft designs are more, well, they have less complexity, many fewer working parts. It's one of the reasons that their operating costs are expected to be dramatically lower than current generation aircraft. So fewer moving parts should translate into more reliability of operations. To your question, there could be a benefit there. I think overall though, to draw out maybe a bit bigger picture, one of the main benefits that we have at Bristow is our scale and diversification. We're having the supply chain issues we've discussed with our current suppliers. However, we are their biggest customer really across the board.

So the benefits of that scale mean that we are at the front of the line. Unfortunately, right now it's really just a math situation where there are not enough parts to go around. I think we are favorably positioned relative to the rest of the industry. Importantly on the diversification front, the number of different customers, the number of different geographies, and importantly the number of different end markets, which is part of your original question, Josh, I think is a benefit for the overall portfolio and Bristow's business.

Josh Sullivan: Okay. Thank you for your time.

Operator: Our next question comes from Savanthi Syth from Raymond James. Your line is now open.

Savanthi Syth: Hey, good morning, everyone. Could you elaborate a little bit more, maybe Jennifer, on the ERP implementation? Just what drove the decision? What gives you the confidence around the one-year timeframe, costs that we should consider around the implementation, and what you're expecting in savings?

Jennifer Whalen: Sure. Good morning. The implementation will require a one-time investment, but we expect it to deliver recurring savings of several million dollars a year once it's fully in place. Beyond the savings, the project will modernize our finance processes and systems with built-in AI and other new capabilities that will make us more efficient and better at making decisions across the organization. To address the confidence, we do expect it to go live in 2028, so a little more than a year from now. These more modern technologies have a streamlined way of being able to get that implemented in that time. So we have some pretty good confidence in that.

Savanthi Syth: Got it. And just on the cost drag, any way to kind of quantify that or help us appreciate what that could be to 2027?

Jennifer Whalen: Well, we're early in the project and scoping it all out, so a little too early to give numbers yet. We will call that out as we go, but we're a little early to call out the numbers quite yet.

Savanthi Syth: Got it. If I might follow up on one of Josh's questions. Can you provide kind of specifics around which parts or aircraft models you're seeing kind of the most supply chain delays? Maybe along with that, just the comfort in meeting the government services, having that trail off here in early 2027, because it seems to be taking longer than maybe you thought last quarter.

Chris Bradshaw: Yes, happy to address that. I'll talk mostly about aircraft models. The list of parts really can change month-to-month or sometimes week-to-week. But in terms of aircraft types, it is primarily in the Leonardo models. By way of reminder, all of the new aircraft going to work on the Irish Coast Guard contract are AW189 super medium helicopters. The majority of the aircraft for UKSAR2G are AW189s and to a lesser extent 139. So really, again, the Leonardo products. In terms of what gives us some comfort on that timeline, we've spent an extensive amount of time in working sessions with them, really in Italy, on the production line, as well as at our bases.

They've also come out and had joint meetings supporting us with our end customers, those government customers, which has been helpful for the end customer to hear the message directly from the OEM. They are making significant investments into their supply chain, as you'll be familiar. They have a complex network of subcontractors that amalgamate to form a supply chain for a given aircraft model. They've been putting a lot of investment into those suppliers, those subcontractors, on new parts orders to help build up key inventory levels. They're also making investments to diversify the sources of supply. To give you maybe just one case study or example there, the windscreens, so these are literally the windshields for the aircraft.

The industry has really been too concentrated in a single source supplier there that's had issues, both from timing and then quality control. One thing that Leonardo's done is made an investment to put a second source of supply on business, and actually now after that, a third, to help provide some better resiliency into that key component. Overall, we think the incentives are in place to get this fixed and normalized. As a reminder, the same aircraft that we're ordering from Leonardo, who by the way is a key player in the European military-industrial complex, are the same aircraft models that European militaries are reliant upon for their defense posture against geopolitical threats.

So we think all the incentives are aligned to get this fixed and to a more stabilized situation. It's just unfortunately not going to happen overnight. Based upon all those discussions and steps that I mentioned, our best information at this time is that we should be at a more stabilized position by the end of Q1 2027.

Savanthi Syth: That's super helpful. Just a clarification, just so on the OES side, if you get more demand, does that come from higher utilization of the existing fleet, or is that through further deliveries?

Chris Bradshaw: We do have a high effective utilization rate for Bristow's fleet, and it's similar to the broader industry stats that were summarized in the presentation materials. However, we do have some available aircraft. For example, we have some S92s that we're moving out of the North Sea, which is a more mature market, into markets like Africa and the Americas to meet customer demand and growth there. We also are taking delivery of new super medium aircraft. As a reminder, we had seven of those on order. Really, none of those have contributed meaningfully to reported financials to date, so that's all still to come.

We are one of the few operators with an order book and the ability to meet that incremental customer demand, so that will provide growth as we look at 2027 and beyond. Then I guess the final note there is, as Jennifer referenced, 2027 will see more of the full period benefit of the contract rate resets that have occurred during calendar 2026.

Operator: Our next question comes from Alex Rygiel from Texas Capital. Your line is now open.

Alex Rygiel: Thank you. Regarding your comments about additional OES demand, do the current supply chain challenges place Bristow opportunities in the OES space at risk at all?

Chris Bradshaw: They certainly could if it impacts our ongoing aircraft availability levels. However, we are managing through that as best as possible. As noted, we have also achieved some better contractual terms, which have carved out risk and penalties for us on certain of those availability issues that are beyond our control because of the supply chain issues. But overall, yes, it does present risk. I would note, though, it also presents opportunity to the extent that the supply chain improvements are realized going forward. It frees up quite a bit of what's been hampering the company's performance to date, and that really opens us up for even better performance moving forward.

Alex Rygiel: Can you speak to the special missions business? How is it tracking to initial expectations, and comment on any kind of integration that's occurring right now?

Jennifer Whalen: Sure. As far as where it's tracking, it is on track to perform for 2026. We highlighted some of that in the prepared remarks of where it did contribute for this quarter, and it is moving as expected. We do expect that to accelerate in 2027. The business is doing well and has more opportunities now than it had to date. As far as the integration piece goes, because BSM is a fixed-wing business, its operations do not overlap too much with the helicopter business, so we always expected limited operational integration. The back office integration is progressing well with no meaningful issues to date.

Operator: Our next question comes from Steve Silver from Argus. Your line is now open.

Steve Silver: Thanks, operator, and thanks for taking my questions. First of all, can you talk a little bit about the composition of the current fleet after the recent sale leasebacks and periodic aircraft sales over time, and just your current thinking around when you're expecting the remaining aircraft on your order book to be delivered?

Chris Bradshaw: Sure. I'll take the first part of that, and good morning, Steve. In terms of the composition of the current fleet, we think Bristow remains very competitive with the aircraft models that we have and the new additions to the fleet, which include those new generation super medium aircraft principally. So a good balance on the heavy and super medium model mix, also on the medium side with the largest operating fleet of AW139s, which is really the category leader in the medium space around the world, recently supplemented by the addition of a new H160 model from Airbus into that medium category.

Overall, we continue to think we have a very competitive fleet, the right mix of aircraft to meet customer demand. Jennifer, do you want to touch on timing?

Jennifer Whalen: Sure. So we have two aircraft left in our order book, and we do expect one of- they're AW189s, and we do expect one this month and the other one in 2027. We also hold options for more aircraft, and we would exercise them only if customer demand supports it and the commercial terms were right. Any of those aircraft that were ordered under those options will be delivered at a later date.

Steve Silver: Great. You just mentioned special missions expected to accelerate growth in Q4 and in 2027. Just curious as to whether there are any particular catalysts or projects worth calling out there?

Chris Bradshaw: Yeah. Happy to address that. As a preface, we are really happy with how that business is performing to date. When you do an acquisition, as much diligence as you do upfront, you never really know exactly what you are buying until you are on the inside. We have been really pleased to date with what we have seen and the performance of the business to date and the outlook both for Q4 and 2027. In terms of opportunities, starting first on the other category, their on-demand cargo business, or ODC business, is really performing well, above expectations.

So long as supply chain issues exist and geopolitical tensions strain trade routes, we think the tailwinds for that ODC, on-demand cargo business, will continue to be good. Then more on the special missions basis, what we are seeing really is an opportunity set, whether it is on intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance, or ISR missions, or troop movements that looks ripe for growth if capital is available. I think over the last few years, they have had limited ability to add aircraft to their fleet to pursue some of those growth opportunities.

I think with our support, looking at bringing in some more leased aircraft, potentially some owned aircraft, there is going to be more of an opportunity to capture growth in that mission profile, likely throughout the Americas as well as other areas outside the continental U.S.

Steve Silver: That is helpful. Great. One more for me. Free cash flow was solid in the quarter. Share repurchases picked up quite a bit in Q3. So I am just curious, I mean, the company has stated consistently that the goal was to be opportunistic on share repurchases, but I was wondering if you could expand a little bit on maybe the timing of the activity this quarter and really your current thinking on capital allocation, trying to balance additional share repurchases and debt reduction?

Jennifer Whalen: Sure. As you noted, our share repurchases are done on an opportunistic basis. We had not done as many of those up-to-date because of a lot of reasons that we have discussed in the past. We had a big capital investment in aircraft related to the UKSAR2G contract and the Irish Coast Guard contract. Those have largely completed, and we were able to deploy capital to expand our government services business with the purchase of BSM, investing in the fleet on the OES side with the new purchases of AW189s that will go to work for customers. Again, share repurchases, the $25 million we did this quarter, again, it is done on an opportunistic basis.

Timing is, we are not doing it programmatically. So that will just, as we move along, and then we did, and we are consistently working through our dividend program and continuing to declare dividends on a quarterly basis.

Steve Silver: Great. Thanks to the color.

Operator: Our final question today is from Colby Sasso from Daniel Energy Partners. Your line is now open.

Colby Sasso: Hi. Thanks for having me on. Can you expand on the key drivers behind the updates on the guidance ranges, noting the midpoint was affirmed, and what risks or opportunities do you see for the remainder of the year?

Chris Bradshaw: Yes. Good morning. First, we were pleased to reaffirm the Adjusted EBITDA midpoint for full year 2026, which I think is a testament to the significant diversity that we have in the business from an end market, customer, and geographic standpoint. Happy to be able to reaffirm that. In terms of some of the drivers on some of the range changes, first, on the government services side, really the supply chain issues that we talked about during the call would be the primary one. On the OES side, those changes were really supported by the strong industry fundamentals and the tight supply-demand dynamic that exists with relevant offshore helicopter models globally.

In terms of risks, certainly geopolitical developments, the macro side with the commodity price, anything there is always a risk that we will be exposed to. Foreign exchange rates are another one that can impact our business, particularly with the big government contracts where we are paid in the local currency under those particular contracts. On the opportunities front, I think supply chain, which has obviously been a big hindrance to the business recently, to the extent that those issues do stabilize, that will be an opportunity to free up aircraft and the business for better performance.

Colby Sasso: Makes sense. As a follow-up, looking at the utilization levels you highlighted earlier on slide 18, if these aircraft are effectively fully utilized and contracted out, how are you thinking about picking up any incremental ad hoc short-term exploration work in 2027?

Chris Bradshaw: Yes. Thank you for the question. Appreciate the opportunity to clarify that. The information on slide 18 is industry-wide data that comes from a third-party source, which we think does the best job of tracking industry data on this metric. For Bristow overall, our fleet is similarly positioned. However, there are some differences. For example, we do have some available S92s that we will move out of the North Sea, which is a more mature market, into some other markets where there is additional demand from customers in places like Africa and the Americas. So we will be able to meet that growth and their demand there.

We do also have the new deliveries that we spoke about, those new super-mediums coming into the fleet, which really haven't contributed meaningfully to reported financials to date. They have now mostly been delivered, and as those go to work, that will drive growth for us and meet demand for our customers. We are one of the few operators who actually does have an order book and the ability to bring in those aircraft.

Beyond that, as we think about part of your original question, which relates to short-term drilling exploration opportunities, we do have the ability to share aircraft to support ad hoc and short-term work with aircraft that might be under other contracts, but we can use available flight hour capacity to support additional customers as well.

Colby Sasso: Thanks for the color. I will turn it back.

Operator: This concludes our question and answer session. I will now turn the call back over to Chris Bradshaw for closing remarks.

Chris Bradshaw: Thank you, Michael, and thanks everyone for joining the call on what has, I guess, been a slow couple of news days. We appreciate the interest. Look forward to speaking again next quarter. In the meantime, stay safe and well.

Operator: This concludes today's call. You may now disconnect at any time.

#3257. First macOS Sequoia 15.8.3 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.3 RCs now available

In addition to the release of macOS 27.3 beta 1, Apple is also rolling out the first release candidates of macOS Sequoia 15.8.3 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.3. Here are the details.

Apple today released the first developer beta of macOS 27.3, which introduces several new Safari features, including Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and Siri AI Custom Actions, and may also bring support for additional Siri AI languages, including Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

Additionally, the company rolled out the first release candidates of macOS Sequoia 15.8.3 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.3, continuing its support for older versions of macOS. Just last week, Apple released macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.2, which addressed more than 150 security vulnerabilities.

As usual, the release notes for both RCs only mention that “this update provides security fixes for your Mac,” with details about the specific vulnerabilities addressed expected to be published once the updates are officially released.

The release build for macOS Sequoia 15.8.3 is 24H314, while the release build for macOS Tahoe 26.7.3 is 25G416.

Did you spot anything new in today’s betas? Let us know in the comments.

Since I flipped my calendar over to November, I feel I can officially start thinking about Christmas. The weather forecasters at The Old Farmer’s Almanac are thinking about it too.

But while I’m gathering the ingredients to make homemade mincemeat, they’ve been checking the skies for snow and whether we’ll have a white Christmas this year.

According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) a white Christmas can be declared when their is at least one inch of snow on the ground on Christmas Day. It doesn’t have to snow on December 25th, as long as a decent covering remains.

Their newly released winter outlook divides the continent into starkly contrasting camps, with the chance of a white Christmas varying by region.

There are only three regions where the Old Farmer’s Almanac predicts a white Christmas for sure. If you live in the Northeast, the High Plains and Alaska, you can expect a decent covering of snow on Christmas Day.

#3255. iOS 27.3 adds all-new Apple Health app, details here

Apple released iOS 27.3 beta 1 today, and it reintroduces the all-new Health app that was first available for testing during the iOS 27.2 beta. Here’s what’s new.

iOS 27.3 will launch with an upgraded Apple Health app. The new app was initially tested during the iOS 27.2 beta, but it’s back today in iOS 27.3 beta 1 and will ship to all users next month.

Today on Apple Newsroom, the company outlined what to expect from the new Health experience.

Three central new Health features are highlighted for iOS 27.3:

Insights tab: “surfaces timely, holistic summaries spanning heart, sleep, readiness, fitness, vitals, and cycle tracking data throughout the day. A dedicated For You section delivers intelligent recommendations tailored to a user’s daily habits — such as practical guidance to adjust a wind-down routine following consecutive nights of interrupted sleep. The app pairs data with dynamic health content, offering educational videos and articles featuring Health app clinical experts.”

Longevity tab: “analyzes longitudinal metrics across heart health, sleep, mental wellbeing, movement, metabolic health, hearing, and nutrition. Central to this tab is Health Age, a feature that translates data from Apple Watch — including VO2 max, resting heart rate, sleep, and heart rate variability — into a metric that reflects how a user’s body is tracking relative to their chronological age. Users can also incorporate clinical laboratory data, such as A1c and LDL cholesterol, to enrich their long-term health picture.”

At-home movement evaluations: “make physical assessments accessible without requiring specialized equipment. Using an iPhone camera and Apple Watch, users can measure their flexibility, strength, balance, movement mechanics, and VO2 max with real-time audio and visual feedback. Powered by on-device vision-based AI models and developed with clinical experts, the experience runs entirely on device; no video is ever recorded, stored, or shared.“

Additionally, Apple says that the new Health app offers expanded language support. It is available in global English, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

What do you think of the new Health app in iOS 27.3? Let us know in the comments.

#3254. ChatGPT can now make animated GIFs with OpenAI’s Images 2.6

Users can turn a prompt or photo into a GIF, then change its speed and edit single frames.

The ChatGPT app open on an iPhone, its dark start screen showing the OpenAI logo.

OpenAI is adding animated GIFs to ChatGPT with a new image model, Images 2.6. Users can make a GIF from text or a photo and edit its frames. Developers get two new API models, and OpenAI says people now make over 4 billion images a week.

OpenAI is rolling out animated GIFs in ChatGPT alongside a new image model, Images 2.6, The Verge reported on Wednesday. Users can turn a written prompt or an uploaded photo into a GIF.

Once a GIF is made, users can change how fast it plays, look at and edit single frames, and share it. Until now, ChatGPT could not make a GIF in one step. The feature arrives months after OpenAI shut down Sora, its AI video app, in March.

OpenAI says Images 2.6 also makes image generation in ChatGPT faster. It is rolling out to all ChatGPT and Codex users on the web, desktop and mobile.

Developers get two new API models: GPT-Image-2.6 Flare for speed and GPT-Image-2.6 Sunburst for quality. They follow the split OpenAI introduced with Images 2.5 in September, when Adobe put one of its models into Firefly.

Use keeps growing. OpenAI says people now make more than 4 billion images a week across ChatGPT and its API, up from 3 billion in September. The figures are OpenAI’s own and cover all image use, not only GIFs.

OpenAI has updated its image tools often this year. Images 2.0, launched in April, was its first image model that reasons before drawing. Last month, OpenAI began testing ads inside image generation in the US.
