#3241. How Wikipedia’s Editors Keep the Online Encyclopedia Human-Written

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

AI-generated text is harder to spot, but that hasn’t deterred them

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor. She also covers AI and biomedical engineering.

Ellia Lebleu is a cofounder of the WikiProject AI Cleanup effort to keep Wikipedia human-written.

Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from Wikipedia that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, AI writing was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia.

When did you realize Wikipedia had a problem with AI-generated material?

Ellia Lebleu: It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this.

Ellia Lebleu Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes, part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology.

Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes, part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology.

How do editors spot AI-generated writing today?

Lebleu: By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI.

Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations?

Lebleu: Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace.

English Wikipedia recently prohibited editors from using LLMs to generate articles. How much AI-generated content is still getting through?

Lebleu: I’ve been working with [AI-detection company] Pangram to estimate the proportion of AI-generated content. I tested it on Wikipedia content from before ChatGPT and found no false positives, so its results provide a very conservative lower bound. In late 2025, it flagged perhaps 20 percent of new articles and drafts as AI-generated. In early 2026, that went down to 15 or 16 percent. But we don’t yet know whether that’s because our recent policies have had an effect or because models are getting more powerful and Pangram hasn’t had time to adapt.

Lebleu: Another Wikipedia editor has made an AI source verifier, which goes through the sources on a page and checks whether they match the claims. Since it is itself an AI model, there is no guarantee that it will be correct every time. But if you want something that works at scale and filters out obvious cases, it’s a good first step. The Wikimedia Foundation is also working on a tool called Paste Check, which can flag text pasted directly from some AI chatbots.

And we’ve seen Claude sometimes say, “I can’t write a Wikipedia article; it would go against Wikipedia’s policies.” If all major AI companies implemented that kind of prompt refusal, it wouldn’t solve the problem entirely, because there are still open-weight models that can be tweaked to avoid restrictions. But it would help with people who use commercial models and aren’t especially familiar with the technology.

Can you tell if the rule prohibiting AI writing is working?

Lebleu: It’s still a little early to tell. We see possible effects, such as prompt refusal and the apparent slight drop in AI-generated content. But again, we don’t yet know if that is because models are getting better or because beginners are learning the rules. The vast majority of AI-generated content is submitted by beginner editors, so we’ve made many efforts to make the rule very visible in welcome messages, editing help, and advice.

What if AI becomes capable of writing truly reliable Wikipedia articles?

Lebleu: That’s one of the big questions we’re facing. When the guideline was passed, it was for very practical reasons: We were flooded with AI content, we didn’t have good tools, and we needed to put a stop to it. But since then, it has taken on a more philosophical dimension. Many people have called Wikipedia “the last good place on the internet.” Being a place that was, in theory, free from AI slop has become part of Wikipedia’s identity.

A lot of Wikipedia’s communication is now centered on the idea that we’re a human-written encyclopedia. Even AI companies find that interesting. It can be valuable to have a purely human-written corpus on which to [train] AI systems. The fact that Wikipedia is still that, and will remain that for at least the near future, makes it a precious resource that isn’t replicated anywhere else.

But will the people who read and contribute to Wikipedia want it to become partially AI-generated if that makes it more comprehensive? We could preserve Wikipedia’s identity as a human-written corpus while also offering an AI-assisted option.

Has Wikipedia reckoned with the idea of “Google Zero”—a possible future in which websites no longer get traffic from Google search?

Lebleu: If everything goes through AI search and websites plummet to zero visibility, how do we expose Wikipedia and show that it can be edited and that people can still contribute? Wikipedia is frequently cited in [Google’s] AI Overviews, but users may only see an AI answer citing Wikipedia. They may not realize that Wikipedia is a living project they can edit and contribute to.

The Wikimedia Foundation is working on an attribution framework that could give AI users more information about the article [being cited]: when it was last edited, how comprehensive it is, whether editors have flagged problems, and perhaps even a call to action. In the future, readers might even contribute through AI models: “The AI cited Wikipedia, but there seems to be an error. Can I make an edit request and add this other source I found?”

I can see a very strong symbiotic relationship between Wikipedia and AI models in the future. I don’t see Wikipedia disappearing, but I can see it taking a very different shape. Yesterday, AI was something to clean up. Today, it’s a tool to help us with the cleanup. Tomorrow, it will be the air we breathe.

A condensed version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Ellia Lebleu.”

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor, where she helps develop and shape the magazine’s longform stories. She also oversees Spectrum's coverage of artificial intelligence and biomedical engineering. She holds a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University.

I feel like all of us human writers are going to have to grapple with AI-mediated readers, whether we use the AI to augment our content or our readers use AI to engage with our writing. Here's to figuring out together how to ensure our words still shine through the AI layer.

You can now use Siri AI with the Calendar app to create events featuring invitees, location, video call links and more. And in Reminders, you can now create urgent reminders for the first time with Siri.

In Safari, you can now use Siri to create tap groups from a list of URLs, sort your tabs, clear your history, delete reading list items and more.

Journal support with Siri AI is new for the first time. You can create entries with text transcription, or record audio entries.

We are also seeing new Siri features for Weather, Maps, Preview and Shortcuts, and will keep testing to find new integrations. Apple is also opening up this support to third-party developers.

#3238. Developers can now create advanced ‘app skills’ for Siri AI

Apple today announced a major new Siri AI initiative for third-party developers, allowing any app to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. The first versions of Siri AI were limited to a much smaller set of supported schemas.

The new ‘app skills’ also let apps teach Siri how to coordinate complicated multi-step actions. These features are testable in the iOS 27.3 betas.

The app skills sound very similar to what other LLM-driven AI models offer, enabling richer understanding of complicated tasks.

For example, a flight tracking app skill will be able to cleanly map what app intents Siri should use to service a particular kind of user request; something that the first version of Siri AI was simply incapable of doing.

Of course, Apple itself has also taken advantage of the new Siri AI foundational features, with a significant rollout of new capabilities across Apple’s apps.

Here’s an example of what Siri will be able to do, from the developer documentation:

Siri can find custom content from one app, transfer it to a specified app, and perform an action. For example, somebody might request “Hey Siri, send my favorite sneakers to my partner in name of a messaging app.” Siri finds sneakers that the person added to their favorites, understands who the partner is, finds them in Contacts, then sends the sneaker information to them using the messaging app.

It’s also going to be a lot easier to initiate Siri actions for third-party apps. With the Siri AI Developer Preview, users don’t have to explicitly mention the app’s name in many circumstances. For instance, if a Live Activity for a ride-sharing app is active, Siri will automatically understand that a request to “change the ride address” corresponds to the app driving the Live activity.

This gives you a sense of the kinds of things Siri will be able to do in the future, coordinating more complicated actions across Apple and third-party apps.

The new OS releases are in developer beta right now, but Apple says the app skills support is only an early developer preview and is scheduled to officially roll out in the spring.

#3237. Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler Is 2027 IEEE President-Elect

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

He has been an active volunteer for more than 30 years

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler is the 2027 IEEE president-elect.

IEEE Life Fellow Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler has been elected as the 2027 IEEE president-elect. He will begin serving as president on 1 January 2028.

Schindler, who was nominated by the IEEE Board of Directors, received 16,421 votes in the election. Senior Member David Alan Koehler received 13,874 votes.

Schindler’s Top 3 Goals as President-Elect Strengthen IEEE’s connection with industry by coordinating events across geography, industry, and technology to revitalize professional activities, especially ones for young professionals.Champion the improvement of IEEE’s digital infrastructure to eliminate manual processes and modernize interfaces.Prioritize the advancement of technology to benefit future generations by expanding and supporting IEEE initiatives and programs.

At press time, the results were unofficial until the IEEE Board of Directors accepts the IEEE Teller’s Committee report in November.

Schindler, an expert in microwave semiconductor technology, is an independent consultant supporting clients with technical expertise, due diligence, and project management.

Throughout his career, he led the development of microwave integrated-circuit technology, from lab demonstrations to high-volume commercial products. He has numerous technical publications and holds 11 patents.

Schindler served as CTO of Anlotek, and director of Qorvo and RFMD’s Boston design center. He was applications manager at IBM, engineering manager at ATN Microwave, and a lab manager at Raytheon.

An IEEE volunteer for more than 30 years, Schindler served as the 2024 vice president of IEEE Technical Activities and the 2021–2022 Division IV director. He was chair of the IEEE Conferences Committee from 2015 to 2018 and president of the IEEE Microwave Theory and Technology Society (MTTS) in 2003. He received the society’s 2018 Distinguished Service Award and its 2015 N. Walter Cox Award. His award-winning micro-business column has appeared in IEEE Microwave Magazine since 2011.

He also led the 2025 One IEEE to Enable Strategic Investments in Innovations and Public Imperative Activities adhoc committee.

Schindler is an IEEE–Eta Kappa Nu member and a MTTS honorary life member.

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute, covering the work and accomplishments of IEEE members and IEEE and technology-related events. She has a master's degree in health communications from Rutgers University, in New Brunswick, N.J.

#3236. Living with Mom and trading on margin. The regular investor gets in on Wall Street's record stock borrowing binge

HOUSTON — During a late night at home in May 2021, Hy Luu, a 29-year-old engineering consultant, was researching how to obtain more capital to invest in shares of Tesla.

That's when he discovered margin investing: the act of borrowing money from a broker to buy securities such as stocks, while using existing investments as collateral. Borrowing would give him more buying power, and he could pay it back as the stock appreciated. The main risk would be a margin call, or having to deposit more money into the account, if its value fell.

It was all too good to be true, Luu thought.

Luu — who lives with his mother, Kim Nguyen, in a three-bedroom, two-bathroom house in Houston — decided to get her opinion on the topic, given that she used to work as an accountant and just so happened to still be awake that evening. The 66-year-old retiree found it interesting.

That was the reassurance he needed, and it wasn't long before he started using margin to invest in Tesla for the first time. A year or so later, he had amassed more than $100,000 of margin debt.

"I went really crazy," he told CNBC in an interview. "The stock was going up, and so I was like, 'There's no way I could lose.'"

After five years of margin investing — including a period in 2022 where he worried that further declines in Tesla could trigger a margin call — Luu is working to pay down his largest margin balance ever. In June, he exercised $165,000 on five Tesla call options and bought 500 shares at $330 per share. After accounting for the cash in his account, this drove his borrowing to more than $156,000.

Tesla swung from below $370 a share to more than $430 during that month.

Between his Tesla investments, his company stock and 401(k) — while subtracting his margin debt as well as other debt he's accumulated, such as his car loan and student loans — Luu's net worth has skyrocketed to more than $800,000 from negative territory seven years ago.

"I'm very close to becoming a millionaire," the investor said. He did stress, "What I'm doing is risky. I don't recommend anyone do it."

Yet, Luu has found himself part of a growing trend taking hold in the market.

Retail investors like Luu are borrowing more and more money to invest. Robinhood's margin book grew to a record $21.6 billion in the second quarter, up 127% year over year and a 332% increase from the $5 billion seen in Q2 2024. To margin invest on the platform, eligible users must have a portfolio value of at least $2,000.

"Robinhood has made a really concerted effort to go after customers that are actively using margin because they're the most active traders," said Devin Ryan, head of financial technology research at Citizens.

Brokerage firms can benefit from margin investing by collecting interest on margin loans, while highly active customers can also generate additional trading-related revenue.

"If you look at the offers that Robinhood has had in the market over the past couple of years, it's been targeting those customers with obviously transfer bonuses, but also very low margin rates, very high yields on their cash," Ryan said.

To be sure, other parts of Robinhood's business are also growing, including retirement assets — which have nearly quadrupled in the last two years.

Another factor fueling the rise in margin investing is easier access through smartphones, according to Ryan.

"Having very little friction in investing and having everything at your fingertips, and then having a really seamless mobile experience where it's not clunky, I think, plays a big part of that," he said.

A Robinhood spokesperson told CNBC its products are designed to appeal to a number of customers, saying that "we don't believe it's accurate to characterize" its transfer promotions as specifically targeting "active traders who are trading on margin or may trade on margin." The company said it tries to "meet users where they are," and they "reject any implication" that the company is "encouraging risky trading."

Robinhood's margin debt isn't the only one reaching records. Total margin debt hit an all-time high of around $1.5 trillion in June, per the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, which incorporates data on both institutional investors such as hedge funds and retail investors.

Not all of that debt is driven by fresh borrowing due to new borrowing decisions. For example, as equities rise in value, an investor may need to cover a short position that's been marked to market, or valued at its current price.

Nonetheless, Sam Huszczo, chief investment officer at SGH Wealth Management, thinks the market's bull run — which has seen multiple record highs this year alone — is feeding a shift in investor psychology, and margin debt is one sign.

"That's greed," the founder said, adding that it's "not everywhere" in the market, but it's "certainly creeping into pockets."

"Margin, that's only the tip of the iceberg of what we can see," he continued. "Fear of missing out is just the emotion of jealousy with a brokerage account."

Huszczo considers the market to actually be "way healthier" than people think. Though he recognizes that increasing margin debt and the rise of risky assets such as leveraged ETFs inject more fragility in the system.

"People need to differentiate between what's a legitimate momentum growth investment and what's reckless chasing," Huszczo also said.

Huszczo shares the commonly held belief among financial advisors that investors' portfolios shouldn't be overly concentrated in one stock or even one sector.

Yet Luu has been zeroed in on Tesla ever since he bought his first share in late 2019. Earlier that year, he had started his current job — a time when he knew nothing about investing, he said. It wasn't until a co-worker told him to download Robinhood months later that he began looking into stocks and other assets.

"I started making money, and I quickly learned, 'Now I'm making money, what do I do with it?'" he said. "I started investing in index funds and even in crypto, and then I did the math. I looked at the returns, and I was like, 'This is very slow returns. I'm never gonna reach retirement, financial independence until like 65.'"

Little did he know that a decision he had made that summer would become his guiding light.

"I was choosing between a Honda Civic and a Tesla Model 3, and my friend, he scheduled a test drive for me to drive the Model 3," Luu said. "My plan was only to go into it just to test drive it. I wasn't going to buy anything. I wasn't going to put in any reservation. Long story short, after the test drive, I put in my reservation the same day, and I got the car like two weeks later."

Seeing the value the car provides in his life, Luu said he can envision a future where electric and autonomous vehicles are commonplace. Because of how much he believes in that future, he considers Tesla the "easiest" investment he's made, and over the course of seven years of investing in the company, he has generally held his shares.

However, things got a bit more difficult with his strategy when Tesla shares began falling in 2022, putting him in the vulnerable position of potentially receiving a margin call. 2022 was Tesla's worst year on record, with the stock finishing off the year at $123.18 after a roughly 65% decline.

In search of more capital, Luu made a serious financial decision with his mother's approval.

"I refinanced the house to get access to an extra $30,000 of capital, and I used that to pay down my margin debt," he said.

Luu understands the level of risk that accompanies trading with margin. Because he's been using margin for most of the nearly seven years he's been investing in Tesla, he has deemed his investing strategy "gambling with an asterisk."

For now, it has paid off. In the last five years, Tesla shares have risen more than 43% to $375. However, the volatile stock is about 25% off of its all-time high near $499.

"It's very easy to see it as gambling, because obviously all your money is in one stock, and that's inherently risky," he said. "But the reason why I say there's nuance to it is because it's a matter of investing temperament, financial discipline and time horizon."

With a time horizon of "many decades," a temperament he labels as "very calm and collected" and a "very high" conviction in Tesla, Luu believes he's "at no risk of panic selling," even when the market tanks.

Still, the situation points out another danger: Missing an opportunity to make an investment when an equity is undervalued. When Luu was scrambling to raise funds to meet his margin obligation, it reduced his flexibility to purchase more Tesla shares at the lower price.

Margin levels this high have been followed by risk-off periods in equities.

Whenever monthly margin debt has grown above 45% year over year since 1960, there were declines in the stock market five out of six times, data from Fundstrat Global Advisors shows. June's margin debt record came in at 49%, but the S&P 500 has still added more than 13% in 2026. A swing into the red by year-end in accordance with this historic pattern would be a dramatic move — one that would be considered highly unusual for the stock market.

The firm also found that the median performance for S&P 500 forward returns following a breakout of 40% year-over-year margin debt growth has been worse off 12 months later as opposed to one month after it. To be exact, the S&P 500's median 12-month forward return is a 4.2% decline, while the median one-month return is a drop of 2.2%.

In essence, the more rapidly margin debt rises, the worse it is for S&P 500 returns over 12 months.

While margin debt doesn't necessarily cause S&P 500 declines, it can exacerbate existing moves to the downside if there's a significant amount of leverage in the market, said Hardika Singh, economic strategist at Fundstrat.

"The premise of gains beget gains, it turns into losses beget losses, and that's what's troublesome," Singh said. "You have these losses, they keep piling up, and then the stock gets sold, and everyone's starting to close out their position, and it becomes this huge train wreck that's very hard to stop, and it adds a lot of volatility to the market."

Then again, Singh sees why investors like Luu are leaning into such a risky strategy. "No one ever got rich by diversifying," she said.

Luu, who said he's been a "hobbyist" from an early age, has folded in investing as one of his many hobbies, which include activities like climbing and playing guitar. It's become such a hobby that he's created his own social media account detailing his investing journey.

Even if Luu reaches his financial goals, he "wouldn't ever stop investing," he said. Instead, he said he "would probably start investing in SpaceX."

It's not just Luu who views trading as a hobby.

Fundstrat's Singh explained that American traders, particularly younger ones, feel they have to take bigger risks to get ahead. She said it's part of a broader trend dubbed financial nihilism, in which young investors grappling with a tough job market and high inflation turn to less-stable investing tools.

"It makes a lot of sense why individuals, specifically retail investors, keep gravitating towards this margin debt," the economic strategist added. "This is like a drug, and I think people just can't get enough of it in this economy."

Kevin Davis, a 59-year-old retail investor who made a living as a rapper in the 1980s and '90s before becoming a stock broker, believes the risks with leveraged trading outweigh the rewards.

"It's gambling. You're borrowing money you don't have, and so if it goes the other way, now you have a clock on your money, and it's ticking," said Davis, who owns an investing technology platform. "The market's not going to save you. It never does."

"Don't play the margin game," the Florida resident warned.

Luu became an engineering consultant because his father, who died of lung cancer in 2012, exposed him to computing. His mother said that between her two sons, Luu most resembles his father not only in terms of his features but also his character.

Reflecting on what her late husband might have thought about Luu's investing pursuits, Nguyen paused for a moment, holding a slight smile.

She then said, "He would've said he's proud of him."

— CNBC's Charlotte Morabito and Deena Zaidi contributed to this report.

#3235. The Ultimate Dividend Growth Stock to Buy With $2,000 Right Now

Home Depot stock has delivered dividend growth since 1987.

It's common knowledge that dividend stocks tend to attract more conservative investors. While these stocks rarely experience rapid growth, they tend to be well-suited for wealth preservation and income generation.

Fortunately, many of these stocks also increase their payouts periodically, bolstering their value as long-term holdings. If one is looking to start building a position by investing $2,000 in such a stock, Home Depot (HD +6.53%) is likely an excellent option, and here's why.

Income investors will like that Home Depot has hiked its dividend for 17 straight years. The retail stock suspended increases in the late 2000s amid the housing crisis. Still, annual payout hikes had also been the norm since Home Depot's first dividend payment in 1987.

At approximately $330 per share, about $1,980 will buy an investor six shares of Home Depot.

Currently, Home Depot shareholders earn $9.32 per share annually in dividends, totaling $55.92 in yearly dividend income for six shares. This amounts to a dividend yield of 2.8%, far above the S&P 500's (^GSPC +1.58%) average of 1.1%.

Investors can likely expect the payout hikes to continue. Over the trailing 12 months, Home Depot generated just over $15.1 billion in free cash flow, well above the $9.3 billion the payout cost the company over the same period. That leaves ample room for rising payouts and investments in the company.

As mentioned, today's Home Depot stock is best-suited for investors focused on rising dividend income and wealth preservation. With a footprint of more than 2,360 stores, the company now adds few new locations annually. The U.S. and Canadian markets offer little opportunity for new development, and past efforts at international expansion failed, effectively limiting growth.

Nonetheless, Home Depot has responded to that challenge by leaning into strategies such as targeting professional contractors in addition to its traditional do-it-yourself customer base. Omnichannel retail, private label brands, and value-added services and rentals have also boosted revenues.

Amid that approach, it reported $89 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, a 5% yearly increase. Net income rose by under 1% to almost $8.1 billion over the same period due to higher operating costs.

However, some of that spending is investment in digital capabilities and expanded supply chain facilities. That could bring efficiencies that boost profits longer term, which should foster continued dividend growth and, eventually, a higher stock price that could make it worth holding for a decade.

A $2,000 investment in Home Depot stock could be the start of a growing income stream.

Admittedly, the company is unlikely to deliver rapid revenue and profit growth. Still, the need to maintain and update properties is ongoing, and Home Depot is well-positioned to meet it for individuals and businesses alike. That makes it likely that revenue and earnings will continue to increase.

Moreover, it has delivered dividend growth in almost every year since 1987, and its payout is well above the S&P 500 average. Given that its free cash flow is well above the cost of the dividend, Home Depot will probably maintain its track record of rising payouts for a long time to come.

How to steer clear of danger while using an AI assistant to shop

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We’ve gotten to the point where people are relying on AI assistants to help them navigate all the madness associated with holiday shopping.

According to Bain & Company, nearly a quarter of US online shoppers plan to kick off their holiday shopping on an AI platform like ChatGPT or Gemini (which is a stat that’s up from 17% last year).

With that increase in AI tools being used to aid online shoppers comes the threat of scammers, who look to exploit those shoppers with fake online stores (which are now popping up at a current rate of one every three minutes). And what’s worse is that those same stores have now started showing up in AI assistants’ product recommendations.

In a bid to learn more about how to shop more safely when using AI for online shopping, how a holiday gift list given to AI could build out an identity map of your family and more, I spoke to cybersecurity expert Serena Sullivan.

Here’s hoping her advice makes your AI-assisted holiday shopping experience less susceptible to any sorts of scams.

Consumers often unintentionally disclose personal information. Depending on the way the user crafts their prompts into the AI engine, some information could be inferred.

For example, if the user is searching for personal care items to purchase as a gift, they could unintentionally reveal the gender and age of the person they are purchasing the gift for. If they search for ballet shoes, they could reveal the age range of the recipient, the gender, their hobbies and interests. If you are looking for gifts that are very expensive versus inexpensive, some conclusions could be drawn about the user’s disposable income.

If the person was looking for an experience instead of a gift, maybe a family trip to a theme park, AI could likely deduce the size of the family, whether any family members need accessibility options, which state or country they live in, and a generalization of how much income the family has access to.

Individually, these details might seem harmless. However, when combined, they can create a surprisingly detailed picture of someone's personal life. This is how a data aggregation attack works. An attacker can pull information using Open Source Intelligence (OSINT), meaning information that is freely available on the internet, to compile a detailed profile of the individual. This information can then be used to perform detailed phishing or other social engineering attacks through email, voicemail, phone, or text.

Treat AI assistants as you would any other online service. Only share the information you are willing to disclose, keeping in mind that other information could be combined to create a detailed picture of the user and those they are purchasing gifts for.

Treat AI assistants as you would any other online service. Only share the information you are willing to disclose, keeping in mind that other information could be combined to create a detailed picture of the user and those they are purchasing gifts for.

Just because AI makes a recommendation does not mean that AI found the correct website and does not indicate that the website has been vetted for safety or security. Additionally, AI could present the shopper with an outdated link.

When you click a link provided in AI results, the first thing to check is if it is a secure website. For example, if the shopper is warned that the digital certificate is out of date or illegitimate, do not continue using that website. Other warning signs, beyond security, are if the items appear too good to be true. For example, if you know an item normally costs about $100 and this website is selling it for $10, it could be a scam.

Shoppers can also identify potential signs of scams by checking the website address and determining if it matches what was expected. For example, the shopper wants to buy a nice piece of jewelry for their significant other; let’s say they wanted to go to ringsforspecialpeople.com (please note this is a fake website, just for the example). When the shopper enters the website, they notice the domain name is not related; maybe it automatically turns into jewelryforspecialpeople.com.

The website could be an exact duplicate of the website the shopper is accessing, but it is not. This should not be confused with related domains. For example, many companies will purchase all the related domains and have them redirected to their main website. The owner of the website could have purchased jewelryforspecialpeople.com and have it redirected to the main website.

Shoppers can also navigate to the suggested website without clicking the link in the AI response. Instead of clicking the link, the shopper could use a search engine to search for that website and click the website from the search results.

Prospective buyers can also review the payment options the website provides. One red flag is if the website requests payment in the form of money orders, wire transfers, gift cards, or cryptocurrency. Those forms of payment are not typical. Most companies would prefer a credit card or payments through other sites, like PayPal, Apple Pay, and others.

Shoppers should be aware of the company they are doing business with. They can research the seller by verifying it is a legitimate company, read user reviews, and identify if they have a customer service department. Most scammers will not have a customer service department. Review the policies on the website.

The warning signs mentioned above apply regardless of how someone arrives at a website. Whether a shopper clicks a link provided by an AI assistant or finds the website through a traditional search engine, the same precautions should be taken. However, as AI increasingly generates recommendations based on individual shopping queries, fraudulent websites and scams may become more difficult to recognize, particularly when the results appear relevant, personalized, and legitimate.

The advancement of AI has given scammers the ability to create highly convincing websites, customer reviews, product descriptions, and chatbots. As a result, it can be increasingly difficult for shoppers to distinguish legitimate businesses from fraudulent ones.

However, consumers can take steps to verify a business before making a purchase. Researching the company, reviewing its Better Business Bureau (BBB) rating and complaint history, and checking for any current or past consumer protection lawsuits or regulatory actions can help shoppers determine whether a business is trustworthy.

If a website appears to be professional-looking, it does not necessarily indicate that the website is trustworthy. If a shopper has even the slightest inkling that the website may be fraudulent, they should research using some of these suggestions or find a different website that does not contain any of the red flags mentioned.

Just because AI makes a recommendation does not mean that AI found the correct website and does not indicate that the website has been vetted for safety or security.

Children would often like to be gifted technology items. However, parents should use caution when deciding what type of technology is appropriate for their child. I would stress that parents teach their children how to spot behaviors or platforms that might be attempting to collect information, or worse.

Many popular technology gifts have the capability of collecting personal information. Parents are the first line of defense for minimizing some of the risks associated with those types of products. If the gift includes options for using a microphone, cameras, location tracking, or has AI integrated, parents should pay particular attention to those capabilities and become familiar with parental controls.

AI-driven toys, like robots or interactive dolls, could record the child’s voice, save conversations and questions the child may ask. Other interactions could also be saved on the device, or in the cloud if it is connected to the internet. If the toy connects to the internet, there is potential that an attacker could access that information.

Video games are a very common gift for children to receive. Games such as Roblox have a feature where children can talk and type to other users they are playing with. A safer approach is to use parental controls to block that feature from children.

If children are using personal assistants or planners and add significant dates, such as birthdays, vacations, school hours, extracurricular activities, and similar, that could be dangerous if an attacker compromises that data. The attacker would potentially be privy to household schedules, how many members are in the family, potentially gender, sexual orientation of family members, religious beliefs, or when the child would be away from home and where they are.

Smartwatches and fitness trackers can also pose potential danger. These devices may collect location information, activity patterns, contacts, and other personal information. Many of these devices are not covered under HIPAA, so they do not necessarily have the same protection applied as medical devices do.

Parents can ask themselves a few questions when evaluating the potential technology gift:

1. What information does the device collect?

2. Is audio, video, or location information stored in the cloud?

3. Who has access to that information, and is it shared with third parties?

4. Can parents disable microphones, cameras, and location tracking?

5. Does the manufacturer provide regular security updates?

6. Can parents review and permanently delete collected information?

Users should be careful about what they self-disclose.

Sharing general information about a family gathering, planning a holiday list, or finding the best gifts for their loved ones is a reasonable use of technology. However, one does not need to include things like full names, addresses, phone numbers, birth date, financial circumstances, sexual orientation, ethnicity, and other identifiable information. Users should consider sharing the bare minimum of information with the AI assistant that will allow it to perform as expected.

Certain information should never be provided to any AI-enabled device, such as:

Personally identifiable information, for adults and children, like Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, passport information, school schedules, extracurricular activities, or information that could allow an attacker to know where the user is physically located.

As a general rule of thumb, if you would not want anyone outside of your family and close friends to know the information, it should not be entered into the technology.

Anyone who is not familiar with technology or does not understand online safety practices can be especially vulnerable to scammers.

Older adults are often targeted because the scammers know their victims are unfamiliar with online safety and security measures and will use terminology to increase the likelihood that an inexperienced user might fall for the scam. Older adults make desirable victims because they may have more funds, like access to a retirement account, which could contain a large sum intended to last the retiree the rest of their life. Scammers will often try to create a sense of urgency, exploit trust, or play on emotions.

Scammers used to craft emails, websites, apps, and other methods of delivery, and they were often riddled with misspellings, logos that did not seem accurate, and incorrect grammar. With generative AI, scammers have reduced the likelihood of consumers immediately identifying the communication as a scam. By using AI and a few pointed prompts, scammers can now craft grammatically correct and spelling error-free communication. AI has made it much easier for everyone to develop websites and apps in a fraction of the time it used to take.

Creating more realistic content, combined with the ability to find publicly available information about their victim, has allowed scammers to develop realistic-looking communications that can be specifically targeted to their victim.

For example, Dr. Sullivan could have posted to an open Facebook account that she likes to take her corgi to the dog park. The attacker could create an email pretending to be from the city that owns the dog park, naming her dog, saying he was being banned because someone reported her dog as being aggressive. They could include an urgent deadline to have the situation rectified, increasing the chances that Dr. Sullivan would click on the link in the email.

When she clicks the link, it could take her to the fake dog park’s website that appears to be legitimate. Perhaps they will encourage her to pay a fine if she wants her dog to be allowed back in the park. Just that quickly, the attacker could now have a username and password she created on the website, along with her credit card information. That information could then be used to steal additional funds from her or start trying the username and password she provided to attempt to enter other accounts and websites.

Voice cloning is also easier to perform. All the attacker needs is a few-second clip of the voice, and they can generate illegitimate phone calls and other types of voice communications. Imagine a grandparent receiving a phone call in their grandchild’s voice, stating they are being held for ransom. The fake voice states that the grandparents must send a certain amount of cryptocurrency to see their grandchild again.

These situations have happened, and some have been tricked, while others knew it was not their grandchild, because the grandchild is sitting in the back seat of their car and could not be the same person on the telephone. If a familiar voice is saying unusual things, it is a great idea to double-check to determine if it was a legitimate phone call or not.

Families can protect themselves by using several precautions.

Tips on how to handle online scams are to slow down and think about the request, who is making the request, and how likely the request is to be legitimate. Scammers thrive on people making hasty decisions or acting out of emotions rather than thinking the situation through.

From the ransom situation described above to a fantastic and unbelievable deal on an item the person was researching as a gift, consumers should take a few minutes to ask for help from a tech-savvy family member or to think about the situation thoroughly before acting.

Here are a few suggestions on how to use AI in a safer manner.

So many AI platforms exist, so it would be impossible to list all of them here; only some of the most popular AI is listed here. If a person is using a different AI platform outside of what is listed here, users can perform a search to determine how to perform these actions on other platforms. Consumers should also be aware that even with these pointers and training, nothing is 100% secure.

Turning off model improvement does not automatically delete existing conversations, and temporary chats may also be retained for up to 30 days for safety purposes.

For specific details, conduct a search for ChatGPT Data Controls.

1. Protect your personal information: Do not share passwords, financial information, Social Security numbers, children's identifying information, or detailed travel schedules with AI assistants.

2. Verify every website and seller: Never assume an AI-recommended website is legitimate. Independently verify the retailer, domain name, seller reputation, and contact information before purchasing.

3. If a deal seems too good to be true, it probably isn’t true: Be cautious of unusually low prices, unexpected discounts, fast-approaching sales end, and requests for unusual payment methods. If something seems urgent, that is an indicator that consumers should slow down and independently verify the details.

5. Verify before you buy: Independently confirm the product, seller, total price, shipping costs, return policy, and payment method.

Details a consumer should verify before purchasing include ensuring the seller is legitimate, validating the details of the product being purchased, confirming the total cost, payment security, and available purchase protections.

Use credit cards for purchases whenever possible, as that allows consumers one more avenue to explore should they have followed all the safety tips and were scammed regardless.

#3232. Why Engineers Should Brave Capitol Hill

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Congress needs accurate technical insights

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum.

During this year’s Congressional Visits Day, Nikhil Jathar [second from left] and three other IEEE members met with Nile Whitmore [middle], a legislative assistant for Representative Greg Casar (D-Texas).

When San Antonio–based software engineer Nikhil Jathar first went to Washington, D.C., to advocate for federal support for technology education and research funding, he was in awe of the opportunity. It was spring of 2025, not long after Jathar settled in the United States from India, when he got an invitation to join the annual Congressional Visits Day organized by IEEE-USA.

“My first reaction was, ‘Wow, I get to visit Congress,’ ” says Jathar, CTO of AvanSaber, a business software company he cofounded in 2014. At the time, he did not have a specific lobbying position on behalf of the company. But he was intrigued by the invitation—which goes out to all U.S. IEEE members—and as he read more about congressional visits, his motivation deepened. He realized: “I need to try this. I want to see where it goes.”

What’s Your Ask? Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:Cosponsor (or oppose) an existing bill or amendment.Preserve, remove, or modify legislative text in a bill under consideration.Add language to an appropriations bill or committee report.Ask a federal agency a specific oversight question.Request a briefing, hearing, Government Accountability Office review, or stakeholder roundtable.Encourage an agency to clarify a technical rule.

Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:

Congressional staffers say they welcome the knowledge and perspective that engineers like Jathar and other visitors from beyond Washington, D.C., provide. It’s also important for those visitors to be clear on what they are advocating for. One staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, who agreed to speak anonymously due to the office’s media policy, says, “Ideas for new policies come from multiple places. It could begin at the [legislator] or staff level, an ask from a constituent, or needs from industry. It’s up to us to figure out what would do the most good,” the staffer said. “For instance, if you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”

For engineers in the United States, speaking with elected representatives is an effective way to shape key policies, but it takes some preparation and the right approach, as Jathar learned over the course of two visits.

Congress’s job is to act on behalf of the people, and it has rules for how people can lobby it. It distinguishes between broader advocacy—conversations between constituents and U.S. representatives—and professional lobbying, which involves paid professionals and is governed by the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Many professional groups like IEEE also organize congressional visits for their members. Those visits can be subject to lobbying rules, so the organizers told Jathar that: “You are representing the organization, not your own views.” He would need to stick to the talking points IEEE-USA had prepared for all its participants, regardless of their specialty, to promote across several congressional offices.

On Jathar’s first visit, those organizational talking points included advocating for funding smart grids, authorizing Department of Energy research, and investing in STEM education. That represents one of the trade-offs of access in Washington. IEEE-USA’s priorities didn’t all overlap directly with Jathar’s work, but they were broad enablers of science and technology and, he says, “STEM education funding is close to my heart.”

Anyone can approach their representatives in Washington with their personal priorities, Jathar notes, but given how pressed for time congressional staff are, they are more likely to prioritize a meeting that represents the views of as many of their constituents as possible. “I could have gone outside the IEEE structure,” Jathar says, but congressional staff “are more likely to listen if you are part of a much bigger organization.”

For Jathar’s first congressional visit, organizers assigned him to call on the offices of several representatives from both political parties based on where he lives: Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), and Barry Moore (R-Ala.). “Meeting a staffer or a senior member from their office is good. They tend to relate to these issues more than a representative, because a representative has 10 different high-level things they have to worry about whereas the staffer can be more focused on the policy details,” Jathar says.

A typical visit like this may last anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour, so Jathar kept his talking points simple and short. “First and foremost you’re gonna get a very small window,” he says, “Make sure you’ve got everything ready to present in bullet points and not a lot of jargon. You can always bring that out later if they ask more questions.” Simple visual aids, in the form of one-page handouts, may be helpful for communicating numeric or technical information, too.

“If you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”–Staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology

The House Science Committee staffer agrees: “I prefer meetings where people know what they want and know what we’re doing in Congress.” In addition to having a clear request, the staffer says engineers and other advocates should keep track of where Congress is in its cycle: Is it appropriations season, and when is the next budget being set? How far along is a given piece of legislation in the process, and what is realistic to change at that point?

During Jathar’s 2025 visit to one Capitol Hill office, he learned firsthand the importance of preparation. For one of the three representatives he visited, staff politely pointed out that the legislator they worked for was not on the committee with jurisdiction over the IEEE-USA talking point they were discussing. “They explained that there are only certain things [the legislator] can do on that issue and that there are other people we need to talk to, to achieve more,” Jathar recalls.

Earlier this year, Jathar decided to go back to Capitol Hill with his newfound knowledge, again within the framework of an IEEE-USA visit. This time he was able to provide something else legislative staff want from engineers: authoritative technical knowledge.

“When I introduced myself as a software developer to one staffer, his first question was, ‘Do you think AI will replace coders?’ ” Jathar says. The conversation went back and forth, with the staffer asking Jathar and his other engineering companions questions. Jathar went on to explain that his company developed an open-source business-management software it calls ERPClaw, designed to be used with AI agents such as OpenClaw. That led naturally to discussing the role of open source in AI, which plays a role in one of IEEE-USA’s proposals for democratizing AI. This time Jathar was able to align his organization’s advocacy with his expertise and the staffer’s areas of interest.

It’s too soon to know what legislative impact that advocacy might have, but it’s the sort of informed, relevant proposal that legislative staff seek out. “The people who build trust have more cachet with congressional staff because they’ve asked for something that’s reasonably thought out,” the House Science Committee staffer says. In turn, congressional staffers can advocate better within their offices for policies brought to them by people they trust.

And talking about the issues you care the most about can deepen that trust. The House Science Committee staffer once visited Congress as an advocate before switching to the other side of the table. On that visit, as on Jathar’s, the professional society organizing the visit provided a pitch. “I was making a pitch that was given to me without a lot of personal buy-in,” the staffer says. Instead, “you should feel emotionally connected to any issue you’re advocating for.”

Jathar’s support for the open-source movement is like that. Open source gives smaller companies a foundation they can adapt and build upon, while allowing other developers to extend that work. “We can progress a lot faster,” Jathar says. “I’m not doing it only because it’s good for my business, but because I feel it’s good for any technological advancement.”

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum. He covers how emerging technologies are changing the balance of power between companies, governments, and individuals. The rest of the time, he worries about his own balance on a bicycle, skis, or the side of a mountain.

I found it difficult to get answers from legislative offices, so I'd love to hear what's missing in this story from any legislative staffers either here in the comments or at my email address (on our About page). I also know that things work somewhat differently in each country--are there readers in India or Germany or Chile who might be able to share their experiences working with lawmakers there?

#3231. Novo Nordisk Stock Jumped After Earnings — But Its CEO Won't Give 2027 Guidance. Here's What Investors Should Know

The Wegovy maker raised its outlook again and the stock jumped. But its CEO refused to forecast next year, and handed investors six clues instead.

Novo Nordisk (NVO +4.95%) gave investors a lot of what they wanted on Wednesday. Third-quarter sales rose 4% at constant exchange rates to about $11.9 billion, ahead of Wall Street estimates closer to $11 billion. Sales of obesity drugs jumped 22%. And the company raised its full-year outlook again, now calling for sales growth of anywhere from a 2% decline to a 2% gain. In August, it was expecting a decline of up to 6%.

The stock rose about 5% to more than $42 on Wednesday, but the question investors keep asking, according to one analyst, is about next year, and that's the one Novo wouldn't answer.

When an analyst at BNP Paribas asked whether Novo could return to sales growth in 2027, Doustdar was direct. "We're not going to guide," he said, "but let me go out of my way and provide even more building blocks for next year so maybe you can do your own math."

There's an obvious reason for the caution. Chief Financial Officer Karsten Munk Knudsen is leaving after 27 years, and his replacement, Luigi La Corte, is coming over from skin-care company Galderma. Knudsen stays through the end of the year, and Novo plans to give its 2027 forecast with its full-year results in February.

So instead of a number, Doustdar offered three pluses and three minuses. Here's how they stack up.

The first plus is the Wegovy pill. Novo says it has passed 8 million U.S. prescriptions since launch, which it calls the strongest U.S. drug launch by volume in more than a decade outside of vaccines. The firm notes that the franchise has a more than 50% share in the U.S. branded obesity market, and Novo plans to have it in more than 20 international markets by the middle of next year, up from seven today.

The second is a Medicare program that started covering weight-loss drugs for seniors in the middle of this year. Since it only counted for half of 2026, it will count for a full year in 2027.

The third is new products. Novo plans to launch CagriSema, its next-generation obesity drug, in the U.S., and a new hemophilia treatment on both sides of the Atlantic, pending approvals.

The minuses are just as concrete. Novo is losing patent protection for semaglutide, the active ingredient in Wegovy and Ozempic, in some international markets, and Doustdar said the hit was larger in the third quarter than in the second. China is already a drag, and it "is not going to go away just because Christmas turns into, again, a new year," he said. Novo loses exclusivity there next year, too.

The last one is subtler. Novo got a boost this year from favorable pricing adjustments, and Doustdar said investors shouldn't expect that to repeat to the same degree. Then he added, candidly: "I don't know that."

Here's the detail that probably matters most. When an analyst at Jefferies asked whether Novo's U.S. weight-loss business would have grown at all without the Medicare program, the company's head of U.S. operations, Jamey Millar, didn't dodge. Without it, he said, the whole weight-loss drug category looked "relatively flat" from May to October. He added that the pill's 20% growth from the second quarter was "largely but not exclusively" driven by the program.

That's a real dependence on a government program. And Millar said employers are still pulling back on covering these drugs because of the cost. "Whether it's Pepsi, Starbucks, other large employers, when they see the cost trend, they move against" it, he said.

Prices are falling, too. Novo is cutting its U.S. list prices on Jan. 1, and Millar said Ozempic prices are eroding about 10% to 15% a year. Meanwhile, Eli Lilly (LLY +0.61%) is competing hard with its own pill.

Put Doustdar's list together, and you get a company that's roughly balanced for next year. The good news is real, but the headwinds are just as specific. Novo's own long-term goal, set in September, is mid-single-digit sales growth through 2030, which is steady but not spectacular for a company that used to be one of the fastest growers among healthcare stocks. Shares are down about 9.5% over the past year, and more than 70% from 2024 highs.

For long-term investors, that's not necessarily a reason to stay away. Novo is still the volume leader in weight-loss drugs: It generated more than 28 billion Danish kroner (over $4 billion) of free cash flow in the third quarter alone, and the pill is selling. But the refusal to guide is a useful signal, as it could mean that even management isn't sure 2027 will be a growth year.

If you're thinking about buying, the February forecast is the moment to watch. A positive number would suggest the pill and the launches can outrun the patent losses. Until then, Novo looks like one of the more interesting turnaround stories among pharmaceutical stocks, albeit perhaps not a finished one.

Jonathan Ponciano has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3228. Why AI Can’t Replace Engineering Teams

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

How to convince your boss LLMs can’t do it all

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

If you’re an engineer, you may feel like your skills aren’t commanding the premium they once did. Many engineers have faced layoffs or restructuring. But even for those of us who still have jobs, something corrosive is happening. You may have heard some version of this:

“ChatGPT answered that in five seconds. Why can’t you?”

Or, “I made this app in a weekend. Why is our team taking so long?”

I worked on a team where leadership said things like this directly to engineers. This was in 2024 and 2025, when the AI craze was in full swing and Claude and ChatGPT adoption was rising.

Generative AI (and the marketing behind it) gives people the illusion that the work is simpler than it is. A working demo hides complexity, and once someone has a website that works, they may decide they no longer need engineers, or start to distrust the ones they do have.

Some CEOs want to believe they can replace an engineering team with a few sexy prompts. Many companies also want them to believe this.

That website works great in the demo—under specific conditions and without users with thumbs for fingers. Then it has to plug into a system with millions of lines of old code, satisfy legal requirements, meet accessibility standards, and be delivered in a complex deployment process.

Thinking that writing code was the only bottleneck for deploying new software is like the Titanic seeing the tip of the iceberg and assuming there was nothing underneath it.

Engineers have a unique position in the AI space, because you have the capacity to understand how these models work much better than the average person. Use this to your advantage.

Learn how AI models work. If you can’t already explain that LLMs are probabilistic, what tokens are, or why training data matters, spend a weekend fixing that. You don’t need to become a full-blown AI researcher. A few fundamentals will put you ahead of most people making the AI decisions.

Teach upward. Turn that knowledge into teaching moments for the people who lead you. Explain the limits of these tools, and why a demo and a production system are different animals. It keeps people from truly believing that a notebook full of prompts can replace an engineering team.

Consider the criticism of today’s processes. Some of what we do has been treated as ceremony for too long. Be willing to say, “you know what, maybe you’re right, this process is too slow for the speed we can work at now.” Conceding that earns you the credibility to defend the steps that matter.

I still believe that speed at the cost of everything else is harmful—but that’s a topic for another time.

Find your voice. Engineers at the forefront of AI adoption need to push back and explain why we do things the way we do. Nobody else in the room is going to do it for us.

Your goal, in my opinion, is to save your organization from buying into the hype so much that they chase the wrong thing. Our job, before and after AI, is building safe and useful products for human beings, and engineers are still best suited for that.

The need to educate engineering students about ethics and social responsibility is widely recognized, but today’s curricula often miss the mark. Three professors propose a new approach: adding ethics training directly to core technical coursework.

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, an online education platform that helps people break into AI and modern software roles through project-based learning and one-on-one mentorship with senior developers. Parsity helps career changers transition into software by focusing on practical skills, real-world systems, and the kind of experience companies actually look for.Outside Parsity, Brian works a senior software engineer in the SF Bay Area.Brian is also a father of three, and when he’s not working with students or building programs, you might catch him running around Lake Merritt in Oakland, California.
